Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

It will be possible to be at ringside to watch Tyson Fury box in Thailand this Friday evening and then attend Anthony Joshua’s fight in Saudi Arabia on Saturday night.

The Gypsy King will prove that by flying from Bangkok to Riyadh soon after his encounter with the veteran Mariusz Wach in time to see AJ take on somebody called Kristian Prenga.

It is safe to presume that precious few, if any, of their respective thousands of fans will join Fury on that journey or pitch up at either occasion. And not only because many of them will have sacrificed a year or two’s wages, perhaps their mortgages, maybe their marriages on England’s ill-fated World Cup expedition.

Even the rich boys on tour are likely to jib at forking out another small fortune to attend distant events which are fights in name only. Joshua’s flight booking gives the game away, as does the choice of venues. No capital cities this time. Fury goes through the motions in the notorious Thai beach resort of Pattaya. Joshua at Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah-on-sea.

Of course these are by way of preparation for them fighting each other in that forever awaited box-office boomer later this year. But to be honest these match-ups are not so much warm-ups as water-treaders. These opponents would be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners.

Describing Poland’s Mariusz Wach as a ring veteran is actually an understatement of his decline since he went into a world heavyweight title fight against Wladimir Klitschko as 27-0 unbeaten challenger. He not only lost that night in Germany 14 years ago but failed a drugs test which interrupted for two years his descent into today’s 39 wins, 13 defeats record.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

Tyson Fury is fighting Mariusz Wach in Bangkok on Friday as he prepares to secure a long-awaited bout with Joshua

The longer he drags on, as he approaches his 46th birthday, the more he becomes a useful punch-bag, given his masochistic capacity to absorb punches for several rounds. A painful service he has provided to a number of British heavyweights, Dillian Whyte, Frazer Clarke and Hughie Fury among them. This is so patently a mismatch that it is not being televised anywhere in the world, but being saved by Netflix to help promote Fury v Joshua when that finally comes around,

Two years ago Wach was flattened in as many rounds by our world heavyweight champion-in-waiting Moses Itauma. That mercifully swift ending made for more comfortable viewing than some of the pointless beatings he has taken down the years. Make it quick, Tyson.

Kristian Prenga is a virtually unknown entity outside his native Albania. He has passed almost equally unnoticed on undercards mostly around New York, New Jersey, Philadelphia and across the Canadian border since he emigrated to the US.

At least he is ten years younger than Wach and has 20 knock-out wins on his record against one points defeat. Not that you are likely to recognise any of the names on that dance card. Try Joey Dawejko, Aldo Callendar, Tim Chemelli, Willie Jake Jr, or the only man to beat him Giovanni Auriemma. Me neither. Most of them appear to have other jobs, such as barmen, bouncers or cab drivers.

Prenga, a pleasant enough feller, made the right noises at his London press conference: ‘A J and his team have made a mistake. They’ve overlooked my knock-out record. They’ve forgotten that he can no longer take a big punch like mine. Get ready for the world-wide shock which will change my life forever.’

He seems not to have noted that AJ is a former Olympic gold medallist and two-time world heavyweight champion. Nor that he is stepping into an altogether higher realm. Nor that Joshua is highly motivated emotionally by this being his first fight since his two close friends and team members were killed in a car crash in Africa which he was lucky to survive. ‘This is for them,’ he says. Get it done early, AJ. before he has a chance to land.

Fury is set to fly from Bangkok to Saudi Arabia to watch Joshua a day after his own fight

Then you can invite Fury to join you in the ring – ‘but don’t forget Tyson I’m the landlord for this one’ – so they can start the big sell.

November is the likely month for Fury v Joshua 1. Wembley the stadium of choice but only if Brent Council agree to lift their usual 11 pm curfew and permit it to be transmitted live to the American TV audience at somewhere between 2 am and 4 am London Sunday time.

So enormous will be the difference from this weekend that Fury is about to entertain no more than a thousand or so locals in a small, screened-off hall. He is donating the revenue from those tickets to good causes in Thailand, of which he has become fond as a training camp. It will be charity all-round. What with Wach and Prenga picking up probably the biggest purses of their lives for their roles as fall guys. But what if the inconceivable did happen?

Not only would the gigantic pay-days of Fury’s and Joshua’s last hurrah go down the drain but at least one or maybe both their careers would be terminated.

Don’t dare mention it.

*Fury v Wach this Friday night will be for private screening only.

*Joshua v Prenga will be televised live on DAZN pay-per-view this Saturday night

*Fury v Joshua is expected to be televised live to Netflix subscribers in the early hours one Sunday morning in November

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua refuses to talk about Tyson Fury clash ahead of comeback fight against Kristian Prenga - with bout versus the Gypsy King on the cards if both stars win this weekend
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua shut down talk of Tyson Fury and insisted there is 'no future' beyond Saturday night unless he first gets the job done against Kristian Prenga in Jeddah.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain showdown with Fury is edging ever closer, with both heavyweights taking interim bouts this weekend before an expected blockbuster collision later this year.

Fury boxes Mariusz Wach in Thailand on Friday before Joshua makes his return against the heavy-hitting Albanian less than 24 hours later.

But despite the frenzy surrounding what could finally become one of British boxing's biggest-ever fights, Joshua made it clear he has no interest in looking past the man standing across the ring from him.

'Look, respect my opponent here,' Joshua said when questions during Thursday's press conference turned towards Fury.

'We don't want to talk about Tyson Fury. Respectfully, I have done all the media that I can about what the future holds but you know our focus is him and his team.

Anthony Joshua (left) is refusing to entertain talk of a clash with Tyson Fury ahead of his comeback fight

'We have been working since January, working hard, keeping my head down, aligned all my stars and I am fully focused.'

Joshua acknowledged the excitement surrounding what could await him if he comes through unscathed, but stressed that those conversations count for nothing unless he delivers in Saudi Arabia.

'I understand there is a big picture. The goal is to conquer the universe, right? But first we must conquer earth. My target is here.'

It is a mindset forged by the toughest period of his life.

Saturday marks Joshua's first appearance since stopping Jake Paul in Miami last December, just days before tragedy struck when close friends Latif 'Latz' Ayodele and Sina Ghami were killed in a car accident in Nigeria.

The devastating loss forced Joshua away from boxing as he grieved, with serious doubts over whether he would ever fight again.

Instead, he eventually returned to training and rebuilt towards what could become the defining final chapter of his career.

Victory over Prenga is expected to pave the way for the fight fans have demanded for more than a decade, but Joshua insists he cannot afford to think beyond the immediate task.

Fury (pictured) and Joshua are expected to clash this year but must first both win this weekend

'When you speak to me about what may lay ahead or I sit down in an office with Eddie (Hearn) and he presents to me what may lay ahead, it is a great opportunity for me to understand where this checkpoint takes me and what it leads me on to,' Joshua said.

'The reality of the matter is there is no universe, there is no future unless I get past this checkpoint on Saturday night.'

Prenga arrives in Jeddah with 20 knockouts to his name, although the Albanian has never shared the ring with an opponent anywhere near Joshua's calibre.

For the 35-year-old, however, Saturday represents the opportunity he has spent a lifetime chasing.

'I work all my life for this, I waited all my life for this and I hope I am going to show the world on Saturday who I am,' Prenga said.

Sports.title: 'I never considered walking away': ANTHONY JOSHUA opens up on his return to boxing in wake of car crash tragedy that killed two of his best friends - and reveals how the power of prayer spurred him on
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua never considered walking away.

Not after the darkest chapter of his life. Not after the unimaginable tragedy that left the boxing world reeling and forced him to confront grief far greater than any defeat inside the ring. And certainly not now, as he prepares to step through the ropes for the first time since the car accident that changed everything.

The crash near Lagos, Nigeria, late last year claimed the lives of Joshua's childhood friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, both 36. The pair had been part of his inner circle for decades, with Ghami serving as his strength coach and Ayodele as his personal trainer.

On Saturday night, Joshua returns to the ring in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, against Kristian Prenga. It is, in many ways, the beginning of a new chapter.

It is his second fight under Oleksandr Usyk's team, but the first after a full training camp together and the first real opportunity to showcase the technical improvements those around him insist have transformed his game. And, perhaps most importantly, it represents the first step towards the blockbuster showdown with Tyson Fury that British boxing has craved for years.

But before any of that, Joshua had to decide whether he even wanted to fight again.

That decision was never really a decision at all.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

He beat Jake Paul in Miami in December, but within days had lost two friends in a car crash

'I never considered walking away, because boxing is my purpose,' Joshua explains ahead of his comeback. 'It's not just about competing. Boxing is therapeutic as well. It gives me purpose.

'As fighters, that's what it gives us. When I'm boxing, I know I'm where I'm supposed to be. It's where I'm most comfortable.

'It gives me direction in life, and that's why I never really thought about walking away. I'm content. This is where I belong.'

Joshua speaks calmly. There is no bravado, no attempt to create headlines. Instead, there is a noticeable sense of perspective from a man who has spent the past year processing an experience no person should ever have to endure.

He is careful when discussing loss, and even more careful not to make himself the focus of it.

'Everyone deals with it differently,' he says. 'For me, I have to put my own emotions to one side because I focus on the parents.

'My emotions can come later, but I look at what the mums and dads are going through because that's what must be hardest.

'I don't make it about me. I make it about them. You have to keep your own emotions under control. That's not how everyone deals with it, but it's the best way for me. I need to be a good soldier. At the end of the day, it's not about me. It's much bigger than me.'

The 36-year-old says he never intended to walk away from boxing because it is his purpose

Daily Mail Sport's Charlotte Daly caught up with Joshua ahead of his return fight

Another source of strength has come from an unlikely place.

Joshua's move to train alongside former undisputed heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk has inevitably led to questions about technical improvements, but the biggest lesson he has taken from the Ukrainian has nothing to do with slipping punches or throwing combinations.

'The importance of prayer,' Joshua says without hesitation while speaking to The Daily Mail in Jeddah. 'Even if you're not deeply religious or don't follow one particular faith, prayer is important. It's something you can take into every training camp.'

Inside Usyk's camp, Joshua insists every aspect of his game has evolved, but one lesson stands above the rest.

'We'd be here all day talking about everything they've added to my game.

'The biggest thing is my relationship with hard work. You can be in one environment and think you're working hard, then you go into another environment and realise what you thought was hard actually isn't hard enough. It isn't good enough.

'So it's really changed my relationship with hard work. I want more from myself. I've put myself in an environment where I know I'll get more out of boxing because I've given more of myself to boxing. These guys push me harder than I was ever pushed before.'

Those working closest to Joshua believe his defence has improved dramatically since arriving in camp. Watching him spar, they see a more patient, more rounded heavyweight than the explosive Olympic champion who first burst onto the scene over a decade ago.

Joshua pictured moments after the tragic crash took place on a major road outside Lagos

Joshua pictured with friends Latif Ayodele (centre) and Sina Ghami who both died in the crash

Saturday offers the first glimpse of whether those improvements translate under the bright lights.

If Joshua comes through against Prenga, attention will inevitably turn to Fury.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain has flirted with becoming reality for years before collapsing at the negotiating table. Now, with both men rebuilding, it feels closer than ever.

Joshua knows Fury will be watching.

Asked what he wants his rival to think after seeing him back in action, Joshua smiles before delivering an answer that perfectly captures the confidence still burning beneath his measured exterior.

'This guy is a f***ing killer. He's a beast. He's strong. He's quick. He's got good footwork. He's got good defence and it's gonna be hard work trying to beat this guy. That's what I'd want him to think.'

Yet for all the excitement surrounding a potential meeting with Fury, Joshua refuses to place it above the moments that have already defined his career.

'It's a huge fight, but it's not for a world title, if I'm being completely honest,' he says.

Sina Ghami had worked with Joshua for years as his S&C coach and sports rehabilitation specialist, while Latif 'Latz' Ayodele became his PT after years of friendship

'It's a great achievement if I beat someone like Tyson Fury, but for me, nothing compares to becoming a world champion.

'You can beat great fighters, but it's different when you're beating them to become a world champion.'

In an era where some of boxing's biggest stars openly question the value of championship belts, Joshua remains unapologetically old school.

He points to changing financial realities, with fighters now earning fortunes outside the traditional title picture, but believes the sport's history still matters.

'There's a lot of talk nowadays about fighters saying belts don't matter anymore,' he says. 'People's attitudes are changing because there are different opportunities now. But personally, the heritage and history of boxing still means everything to me. You can't beat becoming a world champion, in my opinion...

'Unless someone dangles a big enough carrot in front of me... then f*** the belts.'

It draws a laugh, but the message is clear.

For now, Fury can wait. So can championship ambitions.

Joshua's focus is fixed solely on Prenga and proving that, after everything he has been through, he is still exactly where he believes he belongs.

Back in the ring. Back with purpose. And determined that the next chapter of his career is defined not by the tragedy behind him, but by the fights still to come.

Sports.title: Revealed: Shocking arrest history of man detained over death of boxer Hannah Rapp... after driver 'REVERSED into her'
Sports.content:
The man arrested for manslaughter over the death of boxer Hannah Rapp has a long history of arrests including for gun and driving offenses, it has emerged.

The American boxer died after she was hit by a car in Texas on Saturday, with the Brazos County Sheriff's Office saying the 26-year-old was cycling on a highway when she was passed by a car which suddenly came to a stop and then reversed into her.

Rapp was treated at the scene before being taken to hospital where she later passed away from her injuries.

The driver, who authorities have named as 31-year-old Charles Medina, has been arrested on charges including manslaughter.

NBC reports that, according to the probable cause statement, Medina told officers he believed the cyclists were 'trying to flag him down' so he 'stepped on his brakes which caused them to lock up before coming to a stop.'

He also claimed that, while reversing at 15mph, he did not see Rapp 'until the last moment before he hit her.'

But, as first revealed by ESPN, jail records show that Medina has a long history of run-ins with the police dating back to his teens.

The Texas man arrested over the death of boxer Hannah Rapp has a long history of arrests

Rapp received treatment at the scene before she later passed away in hospital in Texas

Charles Eric Medina

He was first arrested in Brazos County in 2012 for reckless driving and evading arrest. Medina reportedly pleaded guilty in both cases.

Since then, the 31-year-old has been detained a dozen times including in 2014 - for reckless driving - and 2020, when he was accused of hit and run. It is not immediately clear how those cases ended. Medina was arrested again in 2024 for deadly conduct in the discharge of a firearm. According to reports at the time, the authorities responded to reports of a man - identified as Medina - 'chasing vehicles with an axe and a knife.' Officers are said to have found him in his yard with a handgun. Medina then fired several shots into the air. After what the sheriff described as a 'short standoff,' he was taken into custody. That case reportedly remains open.

Following Rapp's death, the authorities released a statement on the tragedy. 'Investigators learned that the driver of the vehicle... had passed two bicyclists traveling along FM 159. After passing the bicyclists, Mr. Medina stopped his vehicle, reversed, and struck one of the cyclists,' the Sheriff's Office statement said.

'Despite lifesaving efforts, she later passed away at the hospital. At this time, investigators believe this was an isolated incident.'

Rapp had enjoyed a burgeoning career in the ring and challenged for the WBC women's featherweight title on June 13, losing to Tiara Brown in Orlando. Her professional record read eight wins, one draw and one loss.

Jake Paul, her promoter, tweeted: 'Gone too soon. Condolences to her entire clan. RIP warrior, Hannah Rapp.'

WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman said in a statement: 'She was an exceptional boxer, but above all, an invaluable member of our boxing family.'

Rapp's former rival Brown labelled her the 'best dance partner I have ever faced as a pro' and revealed how Rapp had asked for her autograph before their bout.

'It filled my heart because we were getting ready for war, yet she was still asking for my autograph,' said Brown. 'We fought a great fight. It was my honor to share the ring with her.'

Jake Paul, Rapp's promoter, tweeted: 'Gone too soon. Condolences to her entire clan'

Rapp, from Indiana, turned professional in 2024 and had competed in athletics before turning her attention to boxing. During training, she maintained a full-time job as a fire and life safety inspector.

A GoFundMe has also been launched to help her family cover the costs of funeral expenses.

'A beloved daughter to Angie and James, sister to Tanner and Maggie, a friend to everyone she met, and an inspiring boxing athlete,' the tribute read.

'Hannah was resilient. She was brave and insightful, always pushing others to do their best. She loved her family so incredibly much, and moving from Indiana to Texas meant distance for her friends and family.

'Hannah was an inspiration. Even on her hardest days, she continued to bring love, laughter, and light into the lives of others.'

The GoFundMe page has already received more than 230 donations totaling more than $22,000.

Sports.title: Alonso delivers first verdict on Aston Martin F1 car upgrades
Sports.content:
Aston Martin seems to be happy with the performance of the upgraded AMR26, which the team brought to Hungary. Although Lance Stroll endured another difficult day, with a suspension failure not only costing him time in FP1 but also ruling him out of FP2 - as the team couldn't repair the car in time - Fernando Alonso was left satisfied with his first day behind the wheel of what many are calling the B-spec Aston Martin.

The Spaniard ended up 13th in the first practice session and then 19th in the second, with the gap to the opposition being clearly smaller. There's potentially more time to unlock as the team continues to learn its new package - but, according to the two-time F1 world champion, the first signs are encouraging.

"Yeah, it felt good," he declared after FP2. "I think in general we had what we expected in terms of numbers and correlation, which is obviously very encouraging for the future as well, for next year's car and the future upgrades this year.

"So yeah, still a long way to go for us, obviously starting so far behind, but this is the first step, hopefully, of good ones coming."

With Honda expected to deliver its upgraded power unit at Zandvoort after the summer break, Alonso stressed the objective for Aston Martin was to see if it could match its competitors in the corners.

Plus, as team boss and technical guru Adrian Newey revealed earlier on Friday, the package his team brought to Hungary is only a first step - with new parts expected at Zandvoort and then also in Baku.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"Obviously we need to study the data more and see a little bit of the overlays," Alonso noted. "But I don't think there are any big surprises there or any big deficit in the corners now to the top of the midfield, which is obviously the first of our ambitions - to be at the top of the midfield.

"And I think in the corners we are matching that kind of pace, so we just need to keep up the work. Obviously there are still some steps to go on the chassis side and some steps to go on the engine side as well. So, as I said, this is the first of many, but I think there is a positive atmosphere in the team, knowing that we delivered what we expected."

During FP1 it was evident, though, that some of the unwelcome issues from earlier in the season had manifested themselves again in the form of vibrations, but Alonso said the team got them under control later in the day.

"Yeah, today we had some vibrations on the main straight, especially in FP1," he said. "I think the guys fixed it more or less for FP2, so yeah, there are no concerns for tomorrow."

Whether Aston Martin can now fight for Q2 is still a big question - but after spending much of the season behind Cadillac, it at least seems to have closed that gap, if not moved ahead.

"They are definitely in the fight," Sergio Perez said on Friday evening. "They've been very strong today. The race pace looked also very strong, so I think they will be hard to beat this weekend."

Sports.title: F1 Hungarian GP: Hamilton leads Ferrari 1-2 in FP2, Colapinto crashes for Alpine
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has ended Formula 1’s Hungarian Grand Prix second practice session on top, pipping Ferrari stablemate Charles Leclerc at a slippery Hungaroring circuit.

George Russell reported a "dreadful" rear balance, Kimi Antonelli suffered rear locking, Charles Leclerc locked up the front in Turn 1, while Pierre Gasly was convinced something was wrong with his car, such was its recalcitrant behaviour, before Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto found the barriers. It's just a small snapshot of F1's drivers being all at sea on Budapest's twisty Hungaroring in Friday practice.

Between significantly cooler track conditions and heavier gusts of winds, finding the right car balance on the bumpy and low-grip circuit proved a huge undertaking, with parts of the 4.381km layout also clad in brand-new tarmac.

Ferrari initially appeared to cope best with the change in conditions compared to FP1, with Hamilton's 1m19.648s effort leading the early running on mediums, narrowly ahead of Leclerc while Red Bull's Max Verstappen followed seven tenths in arrears.

While Hamilton nibbled at his own benchmark with a 1m19.585s lap, McLaren's Lando Norris went purple before having to let it go in the final corner, narrowly avoiding a spin as he nursed his car back onto the main straight.

It took until around the halfway point for teams to start deploying the soft C5 tyres, with world champion Norris vaulting to the top of the order with a 1m29.228s on Pirelli's red-walled rubber. That was two tenths quicker than Verstappen managed on his subsequent tour, both struggling to find proportionate gains compared to Hamilton's time on mediums.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Mercedes had a hard time matching its rivals, with Russell initially four tenths off in fourth while Antonelli's caught a red flag on his hot lap after 32 minutes. That stoppage was caused by Alpine's Colapinto, who tagged the barriers at the final corner after losing the rear of his car on entry.

As the session went green again, Antonelli's lap came undone with a gnarly slide through the Turn 6 chicane, his rear axle issue clearly not fixed.

In the final 20 minutes, Ferrari did get a few cleaner laps in with Leclerc's 1m18.877s just 0.037s faster than Hamilton's offering, before the seven-time world champion retaliated with a 1m18.729s lap to top the session. Leclerc was not able to show his hand after being blocked by Russell on his final attempt.

Norris' first soft-tyre lap held up for third on the day, narrowly followed by Verstappen, Russell and Isack Hadjar. Racing Bulls continued its promising streak of form with Liam Lawson grabbing seventh ahead of Piastri. Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad rounded out the top 10.

Championship leader Antonelli only managed 13th after having to abort his qualifying simulation.

Aston Martin's heavily upgraded car was 19th with Fernando Alonso, three seconds behind the leaders and roughly on par with Cadillac, although the Silverstone-based team likely focused on further dialling its B-spec car rather than chase ultimate performance.

But the squad did suffer a setback when Lance Stroll's rear suspension failed in FP1, with the Canadian missing all of FP2 as a result.

Sports.title: Newey: Major Hungarian GP upgrade "just the first part" of new Aston Martin F1 car
Sports.content:
During Friday's technical viewing in the Hungaroring pitlane, all eyes were on the revised Aston Martin AMR26 Formula 1 car. After what Adrian Newey has described as a "nightmare" and a "disastrous start to the season", the team's upgrade package for the Hungarian Grand Prix was eagerly anticipated.

According to the official FIA documents, the new package consists of 16 upgrades, including a longer and more slender nose, a completely new floor, revised sidepod inlets and multiple changes to the rear of the car.

According to Newey, however, this is not yet the complete package, with more developments in the pipeline for the first grands prix after the summer break.

"The provisional results are promising. It's only part of the package, so we'll have some more steps in Zandvoort and then further steps in Monza/Baku. So, it's the first part of our planned upgrade," Newey clarified in Friday's FIA press conference.

How Aston Martin wants to restore “respectability”

Although this first step is already substantial, Newey still describes it as an evolution of the car Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll have raced over the past 10 race weekends.

"It's an evolution in as much as the chassis is the same, the layout is the same, and the front suspension is the same. So, it's very much an aerodynamic evolution," Newey said.

"We were very short on research time prior to launch of the car back in Barcelona in February. So, it's really been a matter of taking a step back, trying to understand and go forwards with this package."

Fernando Alonso had his first taste of the updated Aston Martin in FP1 Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Newey does not want to attach specific targets to the upgrade, although trackside lead Mike Krack has already said the primary objective is "to go racing again", given that neither Aston Martin driver has really been able to do so over the past few months.

“I feel it's been very strong steps, but we're clearly on a big catch-up game,” Newey added. "Is it going to make us the quickest car? Unfortunately not. But does it represent a good step forward from where we were? Yes, I believe it does."

As Newey has explained before, that catch-up game has a great deal to do with his start date at Aston Martin and the fact the team was only able to use a 2026 model in the wind tunnel much later than its rivals.

"We made the decision, rightly or wrongly, to delay that for two weeks or so until we had our own tunnel commissioned, rather than starting in Brackley for a very short period only to move again," he explained.

"So, that was the kind of timeline behind it. It was a big build-up process, I would say, so everything was just on the back foot in that sense. But you do what you can and you just get on with it."

Regardless of the actual results, Newey says the first objective is simply to restore some respectability in the paddock.

The updated Aston Martin features a raft of upgrades Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"These first races have been a complete nightmare," the legendary designer admitted. "Hopefully, we can get at least a point of respectability now. I think that is the immediate goal and then from there we can try to keep moving forwards."

What’s behind Stroll’s suspension failure in Hungary?

Aside from outright performance, the most important factor is ensuring reliability is up to scratch. First practice in Hungary looked worrying in that respect, as Stroll came to a halt with a rear-left suspension failure.

"As you can imagine, everybody is feverishly trying to understand exactly what went wrong and what happened as we speak,” Newey explained. “It's only once we have an understanding that we can comment on what we do next, but we obviously need to have a position fairly shortly ready for FP2."

Newey then clarified that Stroll's issue was not necessarily related to the upgrade package: "So, the area involved has actually not been changed. We are short on spares because the cladding and so forth is different, so there are some minor changes in that area, but in that sense it's very unexpected. As I say until we have an understanding it's difficult to comment further."

Alonso was also told over the team radio to stay away from the kerbs, though according to Newey that had nothing to do with the suspension problem.

"Staying away from the kerbs, that's purely because we are acquiring aero data. And when you're trying to acquire aero data, you don't want the disruption of kerbs thrown in, the inconsistency that corrupts the data," Newey said.

Lance Stroll ground to a halt in FP1 Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

That said, vibrations also appeared to have returned to some extent, though Newey made it clear that he was not the right person to answer questions about them.

"The oscillations, yes, that's really a question for Honda," Newey added. "They can see it on the data and they are working on the solution."

Sports.title: Why fans don't get true picture of driver performance with 2026 F1 rules - but it is fixable, according to Haas boss
Sports.content:
Technical changes implemented ahead of this year's Miami Grand Prix mollified some of the complaints about Formula 1's new format, but these have resurfaced after two successive events at 'energy-starved' venues.

A key question is whether the many layers of technology are harming the spectacle by interfering with the work of the drivers, and muddying the picture for fans.

Although reservations about the consequences of shifting to a formula with a near-50:50 split between electrical deployment and internal combustion engine power aren't new, fresh concerns emerged during the British and Belgian GP weekends about speed differences between drivers in identical machinery. The nature of the Silverstone and Spa-Francorchamps tracks had the effect of amplifying the technical consequences of small differences in driving technique.

Fractional differences in throttle position, for instance, equated to multiple tenths of a second in overall lap time because some drivers had less deployment in the longer straights. This has naturally led to deeper conversations about where and how drivers should adapt, and whether the effect of software intervention in the application of power is transparent enough to spectators.

The pre-Miami changes to how much energy could be harvested and deployed around the lap represented as much as could be accomplished with the current hardware, so real change will be more gradual.

"Honestly, I think we're trying to simplify the sport," Haas team boss Ayao Komatsu told media including Autosport in Hungary. "I think currently it's just too complicated.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

"Like a tiny detail of the driver operation difference that have either unintended or secondary consequences is, I think, something we all identified the need to avoid and improve as a sport. To bring the control back to the driver.

"And also just to simplify for everyone. I think it's very important everyone understands the sport, regardless of what your interests are. And then to be able to do that, I think the sport has to be a bit more simplified."

While the headlines have been dominated by events at the sharp edge of the championship battle, where Mercedes' George Russell was initially baffled by the difference in top speed between himself and team-mate Kimi Antonelli, peculiar disparities in electrical deployment are a fact of life throughout the grid. Software glitches have been cited as a key contributory factor to Russell's woes, but this has added urgency to the question of how much of a role the driver now plays.

Fascinating differences in opinion have emerged between the drivers themselves. There are those who lament the interference of the software in their ability to control the car; others, meanwhile, point out that the scenario is the same for everyone, so the better drivers will be those who adapt.

But if such a large speed differential can be triggered by a fractional difference in throttle position or brake application earlier in the lap, is it fair to characterise this as a shortcoming or a mistake? And how are the trackside spectators and TV viewers to know, when the contributing factors aren't always immediately visible even in data?

"I wouldn't call it driver error as such," said Komatsu. "Because again, for you to call it a a driver error, you have to expect the driver to understand every single detail of the strategy or software, how it's calculated. You cannot expect that from a driver, right?

Lando Norris is one driver who says the best drivers will adapt to the ruleset in front of them Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"So for me, still, drivers need to be able to drive instinctively to get to the limit of the grip, especially in qualifying. Pick up the throttle as soon as possible where he feels it's not going to break traction, for instance – that's the sport, isn't it?

"Honestly, I can't remember exactly why the staircase [the mandatory ramp-down of electrical input as charge diminishes] happened in qualifying, comparing Esteban [Ocon] and Ollie [Bearman], but the trigger is such a small difference. And the consequence is too big… the fans cannot understand, looking from the lap time difference, has he actually done a bad job? Or has he just done something on the deployment that he lost two tenths, three tenths? What is the real gap?

"So we will get there, but at the moment it's just very complicated still."

While the pre-Miami changes represented the latest in what has been a succession of sticking-plaster solutions to the problems inherent in the current hardware, that picture will shift from next year as F1 adopts a progressive move towards reducing the importance of electrical input. From 2027, the internal combustion engine will contribute more of the power, the electrical input will be reduced, and the amount of power which can be harvested through the lap will increase slightly.

For 2028, the ratio of internal combustion engine to electrical power will move to 60/40 and proposals are on the table to adopt a much smaller hybrid component for the next generation of cars, due in 2031.

"Look, we improved our regulation from Miami onwards," said Komatsu. "That's definitely a step better. But then we all knew that that's not the final solution, because we had to balance it. We didn't want to put everything upside down.

"So we have to make a step, let's say, gradual improvement, so next year it's going to be better again. At some point I'm sure we will solve it."

Sports.title: F1 Hungarian GP: Leclerc tops FP1, Stroll suffers suspected suspension failure with upgraded Aston Martin
Sports.content:
Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc topped opening practice at Formula 1's Hungarian Grand Prix, his early benchmark proving over four tenths quicker than Red Bull's Max Verstappen and team-mate Lewis Hamilton.

Leclerc headed Hamilton in the opening stages of practice as Ferrari adorned its 'Macarena' wing with an eye-catching three-piece winglet on top of its actuator, an optional piece for the Hungaroring's high downforce demands.

Mercedes driver George Russell was the first to switch to Pirelli's soft tyres, going just two tenths quicker than Leclerc, which was swiftly bested by Verstappen. Russell was one of several drivers to lock up the fronts in Turn 1, which has been completely resurfaced for this year and was particularly bereft of grip.

Ferrari and Mercedes were two of several teams bringing Hungary-specific updates, largely through additional downforce options for the rear wing. But for McLaren, Budapest was marked on its development calendar for a wholesale floor revision which the Woking-based team hopes will bring its MCL40 closer to Mercedes and Ferrari in cornering performance.

McLaren handed Oscar Piastri's car to its reserve driver, reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, who trialled McLaren's own interpretation of Ferrari's upside-down rear wing, which his race engineer reported was "working well".

Aston Martin went much further still and introduced what amounted to an entirely new car, including a lighter chassis, all-new aero surfaces and a new rear suspension layout.

But the team's first test session with its AMR26 B-spec suffered a major setback after 36 minutes when Lance Stroll's rear suspension appeared to buckle on the exit of Turn 2, causing the Canadian to suffer a 360-degree spin, bringing out a red flag as he parked his car.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Attila Kisbenedek / AFP via Getty Images

After the nine-minute interruption, Leclerc attempted to improve his own 1m19.075s benchmark, which the Monegasque driver had established right before the red flag. But Leclerc appeared to suffer a power unit or gearbox failure in the final sector, coasting into the pitlane with an ailing car.

Unusually, Leclerc's benchmark remained untouched during the final 14-minute stretch of green-flag running. Verstappen, who complained his Red Bull RB22 felt like it was driving with a handbrake on, was second, his 1m19.559s almost five tenths down on Leclerc.

Hamilton was third ahead of the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar, who shipped nine tenths on Leclerc. Russell took fifth ahead of Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto.

Fornaroli wasn't the only young driver to fulfil one of the teams' four compulsory FP1 rookie sessions. Frederik Vesti took over championship leader Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes to go seventh, followed by Nico Hulkenberg and Racing Bulls duo Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson who all combined to keep world champion Lando Norris out of the top 10.

Behind 16th-placed Fornaroli, Toyota protege Ryo Hirakawa was 17th in the Haas. Paul Aron took 19th in Franco Colapinto's Alpine, while former IndyCar ace and Cadillac test driver Colton Herta got his latest taste of F1 machinery and took 20th.

Notwithstanding Stroll's suspension failure, Aston Martin's B-spec made a cautiously promising start in the hands of Fernando Alonso, who was entrenched in F1's midfield with the 13th-fastest time, his 1m21.550s two and a half seconds behind the benchmark.

Following the session, Carlos Sainz was summoned to the stewards' office for impeding Verstappen and allegedly driving erratically, much to the Dutchman's chagrin.

Sports.title: Malaysia weighs up F1 2026 round as rescheduled Bahrain GP plan fades
Sports.content:
The Malaysian government is conducting a feasibility study into organising a last-minute Formula 1 grand prix as the Middle Eastern conflict continues to throw plans into disarray.

The US-Israeli war on Iran prevented F1 from running its early-season rounds in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, though there were hopes that last month's ceasefire would pave the way for normality to return - and with it a possible recovery of the Bahrain Grand Prix over the one-week gap between the Baku and Singapore rounds, the first weekend of October.

But with hostilities in the region flaring up again in recent weeks and threatening to escalate even further, it now appears a matter of days before the Bahrain plan will have to be abandoned.

Instead, Malaysia has emerged as an option for the October slot, with its proximity to Singapore making a logical choice.

Malaysia's youth and sports minister, Dr Mohammed Taufiq Johari, said the government had received "preliminary information regarding the possibility of hosting a Formula 1 race at the Sepang International Circuit as a replacement for the Bahrain Grand Prix," in a statement on Friday.

"The Ministry of Youth and Sports is actively conducting discussions and assessing the proposal," the statement concluded.

Sepang currently hosts MotoGP as its premier international racing series. Photo by: Shameem Fahath / Motorsport Network

Rather than a concrete proposal from F1 management, it is understood F1 has set out the various logistical requirements for local authorities and Kuala Lumpur's Sepang circuit to host a grand prix. Sepang hasn't hosted F1 since 2017, and while it annually organises a MotoGP round, the added complexity of hosting F1 would still require significant work by the organisers.

Malaysia's internal assessment should give F1 management more clarity on whether or not Sepang could be a valid replacement option. But while Kuala Lumpur appears the most logical option on the table right now, there is also a chance F1 will not be able to fill the gap between Azerbaijan and Singapore.

F1 has also made backup plans in the worst-case scenario that its season-ending double-header of Qatar and Abu Dhabi comes under threat, with an option to head to the Portuguese circuit of Portimao, which would be a test run before the venue officially comes back on the calendar in 2027.

But F1 feels it still has time on its side to decide on the back end of its 2026 calendar, with F1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali setting a mid-September deadline.

"It is the duty of a good organiser or promoter to make sure there are plans in place," Domenicali told Sky earlier this month. "With regard to the end of the year, for us that's in place and the decision has to be made by the middle of September."

Sports.title: ‘If you're not ready to adapt, you're not good enough’ - Norris addresses changing driving styles in F1 2026
Sports.content:
Drivers have been vocal about how the complex energy deployment needs of the 2026 generation of Formula 1 cars have impacted how they have to be driven, with the reliance on energy harvesting causing a big mental shift in how to approach faster corners.

Mercedes driver George Russell is one driver who has struggled to gel with his machinery this year, which has come more naturally to his championship-leading team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

Norris, whose McLaren team has only finished on the podium four times this year as it tries to reel in Mercedes, appeared to have little sympathy for Russell's plight in what is still F1 fastest car in 2026.

"I mean, I've had to change my driving style every single year of my life," Norris said in Hungary. "I guess for him it's worked for 20 years, for me it's not worked. My driving style worked back in 2018 when I did my test year. That's probably about it. Ever since then I've had to change.

"I think the more experience you have in Formula 1, the better equipped you should be. If you're not ready to adapt to a different car, then you're not at a good enough level. It's our job, it's what we've got paid millions to do. It's to drive any car you get given, whether it's a good one, a bad one, an easy one or a hard one. You have to do it."

Norris particularly struggled over the first part of the 2025 season to wring the most out of his McLaren on the limit in qualifying, before finding technical and driving style solutions that helped him get back in the title race. That constant adaptation process hasn't stopped yet with the 2026 car.

Mercedes' George Russell is having to dig deep to get on top of the 2026 Mercedes and try to match Kimi Antonelli. Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"Every single race I come into at the minute, I feel like I have to completely forget the last weekend and learn how to drive a new car, because that's how it is for us," he said. "Every driver is different. But for me, my whole career in F1 has been about how I can change my driving style every season."

The controversial energy deployment rules are so complex that the power units rely on machine learning software to control them. It has left drivers unimpressed because the power units are so sensitive to inputs that a car can easily lose several tenths down the straight because of a slight deviation in the previous corner. As Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri put it in Spa, at times it feels like qualifying results are being decided by "computers behaving or misbehaving".

While it has become harder for the outside world to judge driver performance and isolate it from the power unit, and Norris shares the general frustration over how random the power unit behaviour feels, he disagreed with Max Verstappen's opinion that a driver can't make as much of a difference anymore.

"You certainly can [make the difference]," Norris said. "Obviously, some corners get a little bit more eliminated. Maybe it tightens up, but if you're a better driver, most corners are still corners to try and gain an advantage on everyone. You're still going to be ahead."

While some faster corners are now used to recharge energy, Norris felt the reduced downforce levels of the 2026 cars are now turning medium-speed corners into a much bigger challenge.

"At the very fast tracks, like Silverstone and Spa, there are fewer corners where you can gain lap time. But on a track like this, I don't think that's true at all," he explained. "Some of the corners this weekend are going to be bigger corners than they were ever before, because the top speed into Turn 11 and Turn 4 is higher than last season, with less grip. In fact, it's almost the opposite. It's a chance for you to make more of a difference as a good driver."

Sports.title: "You're not allowed to make a difference" – Verstappen says the fastest F1 drivers are penalised
Sports.content:
Following the race weekend at Spa-Francorchamps, and particularly Oscar Piastri's strong comments, one topic dominates media day in Budapest: energy management, more specifically the self-learning aspects of the 2026 power unit.

Piastri called it "crap" that drivers can be caught out by forward-thinking algorithms which adapt based on what they learn over time. It means that extremely small differences in driver input can affect energy management later in the lap, but the same applies to factors completely outside a driver's control – such as changes in wind direction or grip levels.

Verstappen does not want to criticise the regulations every week and even said in Belgium that certain people outside the press conference room could “shoot” him if he continued. It sounded as though attempts had been made to silence Verstappen, but he clarified the remark in Hungary: "No, I was joking about that one."

Verstappen does believe, however, that his criticism was not taken seriously some years ago, but that more and more people are now beginning to understand what is wrong with the 2026 regulations.

"I've spoken my mind about these regulations already a long time," Verstappen said. "In the beginning most people were saying, ‘ah, he's complaining, he should shut up’. But I have to say that the last few races, more and more people are seeing the same thing that I could see coming already a long time ago.

"And it's not about me not winning anymore, it's just because I care about the product."

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Oscar Piastri, McLaren, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

According to Verstappen, how that product is perceived also depends on the type of fan. Casual fans may enjoy the racing, but those who understand the background see it differently.

"Of course, when people keep asking me, maybe it's not always appreciated. But I'm just speaking my mind, because you see certain things coming," he explained.

"Sometimes people say, 'yeah, but this was a great race'. And then I say, 'yeah, but it's not really realistic, the way we are racing'. And then you arrive to some tracks and you're driving on not a lot of horsepower for F1 standards. It's a little bit painful, which I could see coming already for years."

Are the fastest drivers on the grid being penalised in 2026?

Verstappen believes the fastest drivers on the grid are no longer able to make the difference: "It's just your throttle input. By being faster sometimes in the corner, you lose more in the straight afterwards, which, of course, is not how it should be.

"In every kind of racing series, if you gain time in the corner, that's just free lap time. You would not then be penalised on the straight, normally. Where now, you really have to think about, 'oh, I have to use a different gear, braking technique, or the way you go back on throttle'."

According to Verstappen, that is also exactly why many team-mates have been so closely matched this year and why the fastest drivers can no longer fully showcase their talent.

"It's basically just neutralising a lot of lap time, and that's why, I guess, in general, you see a lot of close battles between teams and also team-mates, because sometimes you cannot make a difference. You're not allowed to make a difference because it will just penalise you on the next straight."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

At the Hungaroring, this should be much less of a factor than it was at Silverstone and Spa, as the circuit near Budapest is energy-rich.

Even so, Verstappen believes it does not fundamentally change the overall picture, including when it comes to overtaking. The Dutchman won F1's Overtake of the Month award for his move on Lewis Hamilton in Austria.

When Verstappen was asked on the podium how he had pulled off that move, he grinned: "I pressed my boost button and suddenly had a bit more horsepower than Lewis."

F1 cut that part from its own social media channels, but according to Verstappen it perfectly sums up what overtaking is like in 2026.

"It's very different. I don't really enjoy it that much. Sometimes it's actually very funny where you see people in front of you fighting, they're using their battery and actually by doing nothing, you just pass them. You just pass them on the next straight by literally doing nothing," he said.

"Not how it should be. Also, having those wings open everywhere, you reduce a lot the drag while following. Of course, it's done for the obvious reasons, but I prefer to draft up to someone and then maybe go for an overtake on the brakes or whatever.

"Now, the overtake sometimes is done in the middle of the straight, it's a bit odd. The problem is, of course, that real racing fans understand. The non-racing fans think it's cool because you just see more overtakes, but it's not real. It's not what racing is about."

Sports.title: Russell’s Spa software fault was also present on Antonelli’s car – Mercedes | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The software fault Mercedes blamed for George Russell’s power deployment problems at Spa was present on both cars, the team has confirmed.

Russell furiously complained about the lack of power he suffered when several cars overtook him on the first lap of the race. He retired when he tangled with Lewis Hamilton at turn five.

Mercedes later confirmed Russell suffered a lack of power due to a problem with the software which manages the energy deployment. However the team’s deputy technical director Simone Resta said the same software was used on other Mercedes-powered cars including that of Russell’s team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who won the race.

“The software is the same for all the cars,” he said, “it was there in every car, but it affected George more than Kimi.”

Resta suggested differences between the drivers’ power units could have contributed to Russell’s problems.

“We also need to bear in mind that, when comparing their performance in the last few races, Kimi was on a fresher power unit, which is, of course, always a bit better than quite a used power unit. That will change in the next races when we start to have a fresher power unit on George’s side.

“So, there’s a bit of everything. There’s a bit of software, but there’s also Kimi being out of phase with George’s programme. You sum up everything when you look at the final result.”

Mercedes are hopeful the problem has been solved for this weekend’s race, and believe it is less likely to recur due to the nature of the Hungaroring, which has far shorter acceleration zones than Spa. Resta said Russell’s feedback had been useful in tackling the problem.

“He has been really good at understanding and highlighting things to us,” said Resta. “We have finally been able to identify the solution and put a fix in place for this race. So, thanks to George for having done that for us, for the team.

“Of course, he’s quite pleased that we’ve been able to get to the bottom of it and sort it out. It has been good teamwork. It wasn’t the easiest thing. As I said, with the new regulations, there are still a lot of things to learn. But it’s a step forward.”

Sports.title: Hamilton keeps Ferrari on top in Hungary after Colapinto crashes | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton ensured Ferrari topped both of Friday’s practice sessions, ending the day almost half a second faster than any of the team’s rivals.

However question marks hang over Mercedes’ true pace after Andrea Kimi Antonelli was forced to abandon his attempt at a qualifying simulation.

Antonelli had just begun his first flying lap on soft tyres when Franco Colapinto spun his Alpine into the barrier on the outside of the final corner. Colapinto, who did not participate in the first practice session as Paul Aron drove his car, was not hurt but left his Alpine’s rear wing badly deranged.

The session was red-flagged while Colapinto’s car was recovered. The Ferrari drivers emerged on soft tyres afterwards, Charles Leclerc setting the quickest time initially before Hamilton beat it by over a tenth of a second.

Lando Norris, who set his flying lap before the interruption, ended the session in third place. That marked a significant improvement for McLaren compared to the first hour of running.

Max Verstappen was fourth fastest but, in typical Friday fashion, was not at all happy with his Red Bull. He described his car’s balance as “terrible” at one point and ended up almost seven-tenths of a second behind Hamilton.

With Antonelli unable to set a representative time, George Russell was the fastest Mercedes driver in fifth place. The remaining drivers, led by Isack Hadjar, were over a second off Hamilton.

Aston Martin were unable to complete repairs to Lance Stroll’s car between sessions. Team principal Adrian Newey admitted they were short on spare parts for the major upgrade package they introduced this weekend.

Fernando Alonso was therefore the only Aston Martin driver to participate in the session, which he ended in 19th place.

Sports.title: Sainz warned, Verstappen cleared over impeding incident during practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The Hungarian Grand Prix stewards issued Carlos Sainz Jnr an official warning for impeding Max Verstappen during the opening practice session.

The stewards heard from the driver of car 55 (Carlos Sainz), the driver of car three (Max Verstappen) and their team representatives and reviewed video, telemetry, team radio and in-car video evidence.

On the straight approaching turn 12, car 55 was on the racing line and braked early as car three approached from behind on a push lap. Car three had to move to the right to avoid a collision.

Team radio recorded the engineer having warned the driver of car 55 of car three’s approach more than once but the driver of car 55 explained that the cable to his radio was disconnected and hence he did not hear those messages. He said that he was preparing for a push lap and braked earlier for turn 12 to warm his brakes.

The driver of car three said he was surprised to find car 55 travelling so slowly on the line but he did not consider the incident to be dangerous.

The stewards acknowledged that the driver of car 55 was experiencing radio problems which explained why he did not hear the warning of car three’s approach.

However, in circumstances where the driver was without the benefit of warnings from the team, he ought not to have been preparing his brakes on the racing line and, by doing so, he hindered car three.

As the incident occurred during Free Practice and did not in fact endanger the driver of car three, the Stewards determined to impose a warning.

Sports.title: Leclerc comfortably fastest before car problem halts him at Hungaroring | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was quickest in the first practice session for the Hungarian Grand Prix, but the Ferrari driver wasn’t running when the chequered flag fell.

His SF-26 rolled slowly into the pit lane after suffering a systems failure at the end of the lap. Leclerc’s smoking car came to a rest at the weigh bridge where Ferrari mechanics came to his rescue. “Something broke,” he told his team.

Earlier, Leclerc easily saw off Max Verstappen to head the practice session by almost half a second. The lap times fell rapidly as the dusty circuit cleaned up over the course of the one-hour session, but Leclerc’s 1’19.075 remained the benchmark, three seconds off the fastest lap in the same session 12 months ago.

Their team mates came next, Lewis Hamilton ahead of Isack Hadjar, but the second Ferrari driver seemed less happy in his car. Hamilton complained about problems with his gearshifts and felt the car was set too stiff.

George Russell spoiled his first run on soft tyres when he locked up heavily at turn one. The bumpy approach to the first corner made it a challenge for several drivers. He ended up fifth, four tenths of a second ahead of Frederik Vesti, who drove Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s car for this session.

Four other teams used the opportunity of the last race before the summer break to satisfy their obligation to run an inexperienced driver. Leonardi Fornaroli returned in Oscar Piastri’s McLaren, Ryo Hirakawa made another appearance for Haas, Paul Aron returned to Alpine having also driven for them last year and Colton Herta had his second run for Cadillac.

Strong performances by the Audi and Racing Bulls drivers meant both McLarens ended the session outside the top 10. Lando Norris was almost two seconds off the pace in 11th.

Aston Martin’s long-awaited upgrade arrived to mixed results. Fernando Alonso put his car a promising 13th, but Lance Stroll suffered an apparent left-rear suspension failure in turn three and spun dramatically, triggering the only red flag of the session.

Verstappen was frustrated to encounter Carlos Sainz Jnr on the racing line approaching turn 10 early in the session. He claimed the Williams driver “slammed on the brakes” then appeared to delay his rival at the exit of the corner. The stewards summoned both drivers over the incident and Sainz was called a second time for the same offence of “alleged erratic driving”, and shown the black-and-white flag after the session ended.

Sports.title: F1 drivers have “no control” over engine deployment – Piastri | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Oscar Piastri says the Belgian Grand Prix highlighted how little control Formula 1 drivers have over their cars.

Drivers’ criticism of F1’s 2026 regulations has intensified over the last two races at Spa and Silverstone, two of the fastest tracks on the calendar. Besides having too little power to tackle their most spectacular corners at maximum speed, drivers were also frustrated by the significant impact minor changes in their technique has on the power available.

Piastri said the deficiencies of the current power unit regulations were especially clear on Spa’s long straights.

“Even with the previous hybrid engines, there was a big element of learning, coding and AI, to some extent. When I joined Formula 1, those engines were incredibly mature, but also the penalty of things being slightly wrong or slightly out of place was significantly less, because it was such a small percentage of the overall power you got.

“Whereas this year, it’s basically half your power. So any small differences or anything that doesn’t quite go right has a massive impact, especially at a track like Spa.”

Although he expects F1’s engine manufacturers will find ways to lessen the effect, after half a second with the current power units, Piastri doubts the problem can be solved completely under the current rules.

“We’ve got no control over where the deployment happens, more or less. You can push the boost button, but that’s more for overtaking than in qualifying, especially.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Like I said in Spa, when you’ve got those differences there that you have no control over, it can be frustrating. I’m sure it’ll get better. I don’t expect it to ever fully go away, but as the manufacturers understand it more and work out the regulation restrictions more, in terms of what the code can and can’t do, hopefully things will become a bit better.”

Piastri admitted it sometimes felt like he was a passenger in his car while the software played a far greater role in deciding his lap time than how well he approached a certain corner. However he is hopeful that will matter less at the Hungaroring this weekend.

“Again, at a track like Spa or a track like Silverstone, it’s going to be worse. Here, I really don’t expect there to be many problems at all with that kind of thing, because the straights are so much shorter, so even if there are differences, they should be a lot less.

“But the principle of driving a race car that loses effectively half of its power before the end of the straight is hard to get your head around sometimes. Even in Spa, a lot of the middle sector we were doing it just on the combustion engine, with no battery assistance at all, which is a weird feeling in itself, having some corners with a certain amount of power and others with full power.

“Spa was particularly frustrating, not just for me but for quite a lot of others, because those small differences in the code and what the engines did made quite a big difference in lap time. Especially at the front of the field, I think there were still only nine hundredths or something separating four positions, and there were definitely more than nine hundredths on the table for quite a few drivers from things they could not control.”

Sports.title: Will Russell rebound from his Spa setback? Five talking points for the 2026 Hungarian GP | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Will the Hungarian Grand Prix produce a half-time twist in the title fight? Here are the talking points for this weekend’s race.

Russell needs to rebound

This weekend’s round marks the halfway point in the season. Unless any of the cancelled races get reinstated, in which case it’s nearly the halfway point. Or perhaps America’s misadventures in the Middle East will lead to more rounds being cancelled , in which case the halfway point has passed already.

Regardless, as Murray Walker might have put it, with possibly half the season gone there might still be half of it left to run. And however many races are left, the gap Andrea Kimi Antonelli opened up over his rivals last weekend means he will go into the summer break at the top of the standings whatever happens.

George Russell’s recent progress evaporated when he made his do-or-die lunge into Les Combes last weekend. His deep frustration at his car’s lack of straight-line speed was a clear contributory factor. That might matter less at the twisty Hungaroring but the question remains whether Mercedes are actually able to supply their drivers with equal equipment at the moment. Perhaps more pressingly, given the impenetrably complex operation of F1’s current power units, can anyone even tell?

Drivers’ discontent rising

Back-to-back races at two of F1’s greatest circuits highlighted the deficiencies of the 2026 power units in the most brutal way. The cars looked tame around Silverstone and Spa, seldom pushing the limits of adhesion, visibly strangled by their lack of power.

Again, the nature of the Hungaroring and the circuits which follow should make their shortcomings less obvious. But the criticism from drivers – particularly those who feel freest to speak their minds – is only getting more strident. Even Oscar Piastri, seldom one to rock the boat, pithily and accurately summarised the state of F1 racing in 2026 as “crap”.

Ferrari fancy their chances

Having moved on from the ultra-high-speed sweeps of Spa, Ferrari reckons the Hungaroring is a circuit which should play to the strengths of the SF-26. It certainly plays to the strengths of Lewis Hamilton, who is looking for his ninth win at the Hungaroring.

Verstappen’s future

As usual, Max Verstappen was quick to shut down any talk over his possible future moves last weekend. But the summer break starts on Monday and, like last year, there is speculation he can escape his Red Bull contract if he isn’t in the top championship places. Whatever happens this weekend, he will head home no higher than fifth.

A Verstappen move would have a seismic effect on the driver market. While he may testily dismiss any suggestions he could head elsewhere, plenty of his rivals will be on alert for any indication he could break from Red Bull.

Aston Martin’s season starts here?

The team many tipped to be dark horses for 2026 have had an unspeakably poor season so far following the dire trouble it had with its Honda power unit in the opening months. At Spa, the quickest Aston Martin was over two seconds slower than anything else.

Finally, with just one race left before the summer break, the team is readying its first significant upgrade. Expectations are, naturally, high. But even picking up a second or more wouldn’t be enough to propel them past Q1. How much better could life realistically get for Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll this weekend?

Are you going to the Hungarian Grand Prix?
