In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Opinion: ‘There is no longer peace in Georgia’
World.content:
Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

Professor at Ilia State University and literary critic Zaal Andronikashvili comments on the events that unfolded in Georgia on 22 July 2026, including the arrest of a journalist, a shooting in central Tbilisi, and an attack on an opposition stand-up comedian.

He writes that there is no longer peace in Georgia and blames Bidzina Ivanishvili and his Georgian Dream party.

Journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention over satirical social media posts about members of the Georgian Dream party. A shooting took place in central Tbilisi on 22 July, leaving four people injured, including two minors. One of the minors later died in hospital. Comedian Onise Okriashvili, a critic of the government, was brutally beaten at his home. Before the attack, he had been the target of a disinformation campaign on pro-government television channels.

Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: Russia’s state Duma passes law targeting citizens abroad, restricting property rights and passport renewals
World.content:
Russia Passes Law Targeting Citizens Who Left the Country

Russian Embassy in Lisbon, Portugal. Photo: Antonio Pedro Santos / EPA

On July 22, Russia’s State Duma approved, in its second and third readings, a bill introducing what it calls “temporary restrictive measures.” The legislation targets people living outside Russia who are deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties.

The restrictions will apply to anyone convicted under any article of Russia’s Criminal Code. They will also affect people facing a range of administrative charges — many of them based on provisions that Russian authorities have increasingly used to prosecute political opponents and dissenters.

The law will take effect once it is officially published.

This article is based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe.

What restrictions would the law introduce?

Authorities would be able to impose the following measures on people entered into the special registry:

freeze bank accounts and other assets;

block access to banking apps and online accounts;

redirect a person’s income into a special ruble-denominated account;

prohibit the sale of real estate and vehicles;

block the registration of property and automobiles;

suspend licenses, permits and accreditations;

bar individuals from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers;

restrict driving privileges;

deny access to government and consular services;

prohibit notarial services and transactions carried out through a power of attorney.

Before the vote, State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said that Russians living abroad should be thinking about how to appear before a court.

“We are talking about people who are harming our country — extremists, traitors to our homeland. People who have spent years trying to do everything possible to destroy our state,” Volodin said.

How the registry will work

The government will create a state registry of people who are outside Russia and deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties. The registry will be maintained by the Justice Ministry, which already administers the country’s lists of “foreign agents” and “extremists.”

Information will be supplied to the Justice Ministry by the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Federal Bailiff Service and other government agencies.

To be entered into the registry, a person must meet three criteria:

have a criminal conviction or administrative penalty that has entered into legal force;

be officially deemed to be “evading” enforcement of that sentence or penalty;

be outside Russia.

The law, however, does not specify how authorities will determine whether someone is “evading” enforcement.

An interagency commission will be established to coordinate information sharing between the Justice Ministry and law enforcement bodies. It will also decide whether to impose the restrictions.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov said he expects the registry to expand regularly, much like Russia’s list of “foreign agents.”

“I believe the mechanism will closely resemble the weekly expansion of the ‘foreign agents’ register. It will become a show of intimidation through the constant addition of new names,” he told Novaya Gazeta Europe.

Who could be affected?

Formally, the law applies to anyone outside Russia who has been convicted of a crime or an administrative offense and is deemed to be evading enforcement of the resulting sentence or penalty. The specific article under which a person was convicted does not matter.

In practice, however, those most at risk are people prosecuted for political reasons. According to lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov, this primarily includes journalists, politicians, human rights defenders and civic activists.

The law also applies to people facing administrative charges under six specific provisions:

failure to comply with Russia’s “foreign agents” law;

violations of regulations governing the activities of a “foreign agent”;

calls to violate Russia’s territorial integrity;

“discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces;

calls for sanctions against Russia;

participation in the activities of an “undesirable organization.”

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova said the legislation is primarily intended to intimidate Russians living abroad. Since the state cannot physically detain them, she argued, it is instead restricting their civil and property rights.

In her view, the authorities also aim to silence opponents of the war and spread fear among Russians who have left the country.

What happens to a person’s money and property?

The law allows authorities to freeze a person’s funds and other assets. Formally, this does not amount to confiscation, since ownership does not transfer to the state. In practice, however, it would make it much more difficult for people to manage or dispose of their property.

All payments, including pensions, would be redirected to a special ruble-denominated account. The rules governing access to and use of those funds will be determined later by the Central Bank of Russia. Court costs and other financial penalties could also be deducted directly from the same account.

People included in the registry would be barred from selling real estate or vehicles. They would also be unable to register ownership of newly acquired property or register a vehicle.

In addition, banks would block their access to mobile banking apps and online accounts, making routine bank transfers impossible. Banks would also be allowed to deny them loans and other forms of credit.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina described the measures as a tool of financial pressure.

“It creates a paradoxical situation. A person is deprived of access to the very financial tools needed to fulfill the obligations that led to their inclusion in the registry,” she said.

Restrictions on business and employment

People included in the registry would be barred from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers.

If their profession requires a license, authorities would refuse to issue a new one. Existing licenses could also be suspended until the individual is removed from the registry.

The government would also be able to suspend permits and accreditations that have already been granted.

Driver’s licenses would not be revoked outright. However, the right to drive would be suspended until the person is removed from the registry.

Ban on powers of attorney and access to government services

People included in the registry would no longer be able to use an enhanced qualified electronic signature. Existing certificates could be revoked, and new ones would not be issued.

They would also lose access to Russia’s Gosuslugi online government services portal, making it impossible to submit applications, process official documents, or access federal and regional public services online.

Before carrying out any notarial act, Russian notaries would be required to check the registry. If a person’s name appears on the list, the notary would be obligated to refuse service.

The law would also prohibit anyone from carrying out transactions on behalf of a listed individual under a power of attorney. In practice, this would deprive Russians living abroad of one of the main ways to manage their property and handle legal matters in Russia remotely.

Which consular services would be denied?

One of the law’s most significant restrictions concerns Russian consulates abroad. People included in the registry would lose access to nearly all consular services.

They would no longer be able to:

obtain a new international passport;

notarize a power of attorney;

certify copies of documents or authenticate signatures;

obtain notarized consent required for legal transactions;

register a marriage or a legal name change through a consulate;

receive consular assistance if detained abroad;

rely on Russia for emergency consular assistance while overseas.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina said the most consequential provisions are the ban on representation through a power of attorney and the restrictions on consular services. Those are the mechanisms that allow Russians living abroad to handle most legal matters remotely.

At present, even people held administratively liable can still obtain a new international passport through a Russian consulate. Those charged with or convicted of criminal offenses also retain access to some consular services.

Once the law takes effect, however, obtaining official documents without returning to Russia will become significantly more difficult.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov described the initiative as a form of de facto deprivation of citizenship.

“Citizenship technically remains, but a person is no longer able to exercise the rights that come with being a citizen,” he said.

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova agreed with that assessment. In her view, the law would leave affected individuals in a situation approaching statelessness, as the Russian state would effectively cease providing them with documentation and legal assistance.

What is the “humanitarian allowance”?

The law provides for what it calls a humanitarian allowance. The payment may be granted if a person included in the registry has close relatives who are financially dependent on them.

Eligible relatives include parents, a spouse, or children who have no independent source of income. The allowance would be paid monthly using the person’s own frozen funds.

The decision to grant the payment would be made by the interagency commission, while the amount would be set by the Russian government in coordination with the Central Bank.

When would the restrictions take effect?

The restrictions would come into force the day after a person’s name is added to the registry.

In theory, a person could be removed from the registry in several circumstances:

if a court overturns or revises the underlying decision;

if the person begins serving their sentence or complies with the penalty;

if the person returns to Russia;

if the person dies.

If the Justice Ministry fails to remove someone from the registry without justification, that person may file a request for review. The ministry must issue a decision within 20 working days, and its refusal can be challenged in court.

In practice, however, not all penalties can be served remotely. For example, a prison sentence cannot be served from abroad. As a result, anyone convicted and sentenced to imprisonment would have no realistic way to be removed from the registry without returning to Russia.

Administrative penalties present a different paradox. A person on the registry would face restrictions on banking services while also being barred from appointing a representative under a power of attorney. It therefore remains unclear how they would be able to pay an administrative fine and secure their removal from the registry.

What do lawyers recommend for those at risk?

The law will take effect once it is officially published. Lawyers advise people who could potentially be affected to resolve key property and documentation issues before it comes into force.

In particular, they recommend:

settling matters related to real estate and vehicles in Russia in advance;

obtaining notarized copies of Russian documents;

securing apostilles for school certificates, university diplomas, and civil status documents;

renewing international passports while they can still obtain long-validity documents;

withdrawing funds from Russian bank accounts and deposits;

obtaining apostilled certificates confirming the absence of a criminal record and their driving history.

Once a person is added to the registry, many of these steps would no longer be possible.

exchange

World.title: ‘Unsolved crimes are being passed off as suicides’: Armenian soldier’s death sparks questions
World.content:
Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

A serviceman has died at an Armenian military base. Investigators found the body of 20-year-old conscript Narek Torosyan on July 21. The Investigative Committee released only limited information after the incident. It said authorities had opened a criminal case and launched an investigation.

The committee later charged two of Torosyan’s fellow servicemen with driving him to suicide through negligence. One is a junior sergeant and the other a private. Authorities have placed both men under arrest.

The Ministry of Defence has made no public statement about the soldier’s death. Human rights activists and politicians have condemned the ministry’s silence.

Among them was human rights defender Zhanna Aleksanyan, who regularly raises concerns about human rights violations in the armed forces. She wrote on social media that Defence Minister Suren Papikyan ultimately bears responsibility for the lives of servicemen.

“The minister remains strikingly detached when soldiers die. At the end of each year, he tries to downplay the numbers, but no genuine effort exists to reduce the death toll,” she said.

According to official figures, eight servicemen have died since the beginning of 2026.

What we know so far

Armenian media report that Narek came from the town of Charentsavan and was a fourth-year student at the Russian-Armenian University. He hoped to become a sports journalist. The army drafted him in January 2026. Shortly before the incident, he had gone home on leave and visited his family. Reports also identify Chambarak as his duty station.

Authorities have not disclosed where the incident took place or what exactly happened.

According to a version published by several local media outlets, other servicemen severely beat the soldier before he took his own life.

Charentsavan Mayor Hakob Shahgeldyan also told reporters that, according to the information available to him, Narek had died by suicide. However, the mayor provided no further details.

Comments

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan wrote:

“The Ministry of Defence remains silent about the death of 20-year-old serviceman Narek Torosyan.

The minister has still offered no explanation or clarification. Did he visit the military unit to find out what happened and why? I am certain he did not. He bears responsibility for the life of every serviceman, and he is accountable to both their families and society.

I cannot accept the ‘suicide’ version circulating in the media. Journalists may learn that a serviceman has died, but they cannot know the circumstances of his death. Law enforcement agencies often leak such versions to the press. They later use those same reports to support their own conclusion that it was ‘suicide.’

And in the army, most ‘suicides’ are in fact unsolved murders.”

Tigran Abrahamyan, an opposition MP from the I Have Honour alliance, wrote on social media:

“Soldier Narek Torosyan, who died following the incident at the Chambarak military base, was my student. […]

Narek was a kind, gentle person with outstanding personal qualities. Both students and lecturers respected and cared for him.

Given the sensitivity of the case, I do not want to comment on the different versions or discuss the information available to me.

One thing is clear, however. The state has failed to ensure proper discipline, maintain a healthy psychological environment in military units, and provide effective oversight. That failure ultimately leads to incidents like this.

The authorities must carry out an objective and comprehensive investigation and take steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.”

Mané Tandilyan, founder of the Country to Live party, said:

“Do not say that incidents like this are inevitable in the army. We must not accept such an attitude. After so many losses, it is unacceptable that we continue to lose our young people in peacetime.

How do officers demonstrate accountability? How has violence and cruelty become so deeply rooted among 18- to 20-year-olds that it repeatedly leads to deaths? What is the army doing to foster mutual respect, discipline and responsibility?

What is especially alarming is that intolerance and aggression are becoming increasingly visible in society. And yes, much of the responsibility lies with the country’s top leadership, which speaks to society in a language that fuels division, hostility and hatred. That atmosphere eventually seeps into people’s everyday relationships.

We must overcome this nightmare. Let us each begin with the people around us.”

Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

World.title: NT government opens door to AI industry powered by Beetaloo gas
World.content:
As the AI industry arrives in the Northern Territory, Australia's most isolated and least populated jurisdiction wants to grow its gas and data sectors at the same time.

The NT government has thrown its support behind both industries as 12 data centre proponents eye a range of locations from rural blocks near Darwin to vast cattle stations.

The companies have arrived just in time to take advantage of natural gas due to flow from the Beetaloo Basin later this year.

It has sparked alarm from environmental campaigners, who say it will undermine Australia's climate targets.

A gas-fired data centre boom would also take place shortly after the federal government outlined expectations that new data centres and AI infrastructure supported the energy transition.

Water use is also front of mind for green groups and the cattle industry, which holds "great concern" that an AI revolution could put extra pressure on remote infrastructure.

Gas-fired tech industry

Development of gas fields in the Beetaloo Basin has helped trigger a rush of data centre proposals, which recently prompted government minister Robyn Cahill to claim the Territory could become the "data centre capital of the globe".

Data centres require considerable amounts of constant power, and developers are keen on the prospect of consistent gas flows from the Beetaloo, 500 kilometres south-east of Darwin.

Is the NT ready for an AI boom? The NT's sunny skies, natural gas reserves and proximity to Asia have caught the attention of a dozen data centre developers.

The industry's momentum is so great, gas company Beetaloo Energy has launched a wholly owned subsidiary, Beetaloo Digital. The company was given exclusive planning rights for a parcel of land near Darwin by the NT government for a 2-gigawatt data centre worth $40 billion.

Another proposal, put forward by Energy North for the remote Murranji Station, would use solar and gas-fired energy to generate 1 gigawatt of power.

The power requirements of both are significantly higher than the total peak demand of the Darwin-Katherine power grid.

Environment Centre NT rural areas campaigner Pauline Cass said outer-Darwin residents, like herself, were worried about the environmental consequences.

Pauline Cass is concerned about heavy industry and data centres in Darwin's rural area. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

"How are they going to get their power? How are they going to get their water?" she said.

"I'd say the majority of people are against hydraulic fracturing for shale gas.

" [Data centres] are enabling another industry that we're opposed to. "

The federal government is working on new AI laws which would ensure large data centres minimise water usage and underwrite or supply their own power to ease pressure on local grids.

Energy North chief executive Scott Criddle said government policy lined up with the company's strategy for its Murranji plans.

Scott Criddle says solar power will be a key part of Energy North's NT facility. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"I think we're basically hitting every one of the government's policies," he said.

"We're not taking from the grid. We're building our own energy source and basically doing it behind the meter, which is what we think long-term is the right strategy."

He said the project would eventually source most of its power from a 6,000–7,000-hectare solar farm, but gas would be the primary source of power at first.

Beetaloo Energy managing director Alex Underwood said the company would consider varied power generation options but could not say what proportion would be renewable.

"I actually think these two industries could be working very closely together to make it happen," he said.

Cattlemen watching closely

Data centres also require large volumes of water to ensure they do not overheat, with Energy North's operation requiring up to 4 gigalitres per year.

Loading Instagram content

The NT government is confident it has strong water supply and regulation, with minister Robyn Cahill going as far as to say the Earth's axis is disrupted by substantial wet seasons — a claim later debunked on ABC radio.

NT Cattlemen's Association chief executive Romy Carey said managing possible competition for water was a key priority for cattle producers.

"We've got quite well-established water allocation and licensing frameworks here in the Territory," she said.

"Any data centre seeking to access ground water … would be required to undergo that statutory assessment process, in that [process] existing users must be considered."

Energy North said the 4 gigalitre figure was a "worst-case scenario".

Ms Carey said the race to build the operations could further burden the Territory's "fragile" road network and scarce health services, as thousands of workers flocked to the region.

"Adding significant extra freight to those networks, and the damage that will do to them … is of great concern," she said.

"It's already quite difficult to get GP appointments in regional areas, so adding additional workforces in the thousands … is also of concern."

The road ahead for the NT's burgeoning data centre industry is long, and development will take years, but likely hurdles and public expectations have already come into view.

World.title: Coalition challenged by rise of One Nation in Victoria's east
World.content:
After years running pubs, the cost of doing business has become too much for Jodie Hamill.

She's sold up, and now she's turning to One Nation to fix her problems.

Speaking to the ABC at a cafe in the Victorian town of Sale as Liberal leader Jess Wilson swept through, she blamed the major parties for making life more difficult.

"Living in the country, I don't know anyone that's going to vote Liberal or Labor anymore. They're wanting to vote One Nation and give 'em a go,'' she said.

It's a sentiment echoed throughout rural and regional Victoria — and indeed suburban Australia — and one that will make this November's Victorian election particularly complex.

For both the Labor government trying to retain power, and a Coalition looking to end 12 years in opposition, One Nation's rise has thrown plans into disarray.

Published polling shows One Nation attracting at least a quarter of Victorian voters.

The four state seats in Gippsland — Morwell, Gippsland South and Gippsland East, which are held by the Nationals, and Narracan, which is held by the Liberals — are particularly vulnerable to a One Nation campaign, Coalition MPs and insiders agree, with the seat of Morwell dubbed "ground zero" for One Nation.

One Nation's grand ambitions in eastern Victoria

Baw Baw Councillor and One Nation executive member Ben Lucas has set the bar high for the party's chances in November.

Speaking as a local councillor, Cr Lucas said he expected the party would win all four Gippsland seats as well as two spots in the Eastern Victoria Region in the upper house.

"I'm not cocky about it. It's just all the sentiment. Social media is the closest media to the people, and when you go through the comment section, the comment section never lies,'' Cr Lucas told the ABC.

Baw Baw Shire councillor Ben Lucas says he expects Gippsland voters to turn to One Nation at the next election. (Facebook)

One Nation is yet to announce a single candidate for Victoria, but Cr Lucas has put his hand up to run.

The party's policy offering is also sparse. Cr Lucas says this is deliberate, and says a short sharp campaign in this year's South Australian election yielded seven seats and plenty of success.

"Election fatigue is so real. Everyone's over it already '' he said.

"Everyone's just sick of being bullshitted to … [South Australia] was a real effective short sharp campaign, and I reckon we'll do the same thing."

Gippsland voters polling to reject major parties

With no Victorian policies One Nation presents a campaign challenge for Labor and the Coalition, which are now fighting against a vibe.

Former Labor official turned pollster Kosmos Samaras said One Nation did not necessarily need policies to win votes.

"Really it's about the brand and what it represents. And it represents a vehicle for these Victorians to really send a message that they are sick of the two-party system,'' he said.

The closure of coal mines, power plants and timber mills in Gippsland have contributed to economic decline, and the government is blamed for the changes.

The winding down of traditional industries such as timber logging has devastated small towns reliant on the jobs they once provided. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery )

"Ground zero for One Nation support is in the state seat of Morwell, obviously where that has been significant economic upheaval over the last 20 years and that's where we would expect One Nation's primary vote to be extremely high,'' Mr Samaras said.

Mr Samaras said incumbency may save some MPs, particularly Nationals leader Danny O'Brien in Gippsland South, but with Tim Bull retiring in Gippsland East the path for One Nation was easier.

In Gippsland East, the Nationals have picked Bairnsdale teacher Gemma Rendell to succeed Mr Bull.

Gemma Rendell was announced as the Nationals candidate for Gippsland East last month. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

Ms Rendell has long held ambitions for community leadership. She's also a proud hunter, who shoots for food and to kill invasive species.

A recent poll by Redbridge found One Nation was attracting 32 per cent of the primary vote in the Eastern Victorian upper house region — which covers all of Gippsland. The Coalition were on 28 per cent and Labor on 22 per cent.

Coalition digs in against One Nation rise

Liberal Leader Jess Wilson is aiming to break a 12-year Labor government in November and this week visited the Gippsland seats as part of her "fresh start tour" where she's visited all 88 electorates during the winter break.

The ABC tagged along for several events where Wilson was warmly welcomed, but most of the tour was heavily curated and there was little interaction with voters on the street. Instead she met with businesses, including friendly cafes and even a toy store.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson has been campaigning in Gippsland this week, but faces a challenge from a rising One Nation. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

Former publican Jodie Hamill warmly greeted Ms Wilson in Sale and was photographed alongside her, with the photo posted on the opposition leader's Facebook page.

Danny O'Brien admits his party is facing a new challenge from One Nation.

"I think it's a real threat. Absolutely, we understand people are angry. We understand people are frustrated with the major parties,'' Mr O'Brien said.

But he says, and hopes, as the election draws closer, voters' minds will focus on who they actually want to run the government.

"People need to consider that they want to get rid of Jacinta Allan and Labor, they need to vote for the Nationals and Liberals," he said.

"Other parties are parties of protest and grievance, and don't necessarily have a solution.

"I mean, who is the leader? Who is the candidate? What are the policies for Victoria?

"Sure, you can be against or concerned about immigration, for example, but that's not something the Victorian government has control over."

Convincing fed up voters of these details will go a long way to determine who wins in November.

World.title: The key figures in ICAC investigation that could change NSW Liberals forever
World.content:
It was a mild early evening in late June 2022, when a Liberal MP stood up to make a speech that may change the party forever.

Without fanfare, at a time of day that few people were watching the goings-on in the green-hued Legislative Assembly, Kellyville MP Ray Williams made an explosive allegation; that disgraced property developer Jean Nassif had funded members of the Liberal Party to stack the Hills Shire Council with people favourable to his developments.

Mr Williams named a series of Liberal operatives and a sitting MP as potentially implicated in the bribery and council-stacking scheme.

"This issue must be investigated," he told the NSW parliament.

Kellyville MP Ray Williams raised his concerns in parliament. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

About four years and eight days later, the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) made public the worst-kept secret on Macquarie Street, that the powerful integrity watchdog had, indeed, taken up the call.

"What I said in parliament four years ago had nothing to do with factions," Mr Williams told the ABC.

" It had everything to do with bad people in the Liberal Party doing the wrong thing, and there is no place for bad people in any political party, or bad people having a role in selecting members for local, state or federal parliament. "

ICAC's investigation, codenamed Operation Rosny, has gone well beyond the allegations made by Mr Williams in his short but seismic speech.

The ICAC will hold eight weeks of hearings. (ABC News)

What ICAC's Operation Rosny will investigate

Eight weeks of public hearings starting on Monday will examine:

Whether political donations were sought or made by some NSW Liberal Party operatives in breach of electoral laws

Whether Catholic Schools NSW made donations, arranged and approved by chief executive Dallas McInerney, without disclosing them and above donation caps to help fund Liberal Party branch-stacking

Whether company Paslibdan made donations in breach of electoral laws on behalf of hotelier Michael O'Hara to help fund branch-stacking

Whether Mr Nassif made donations in breach of electoral laws to help fund branch-stacking in return for favours, including damaging people's careers

Whether former Strathfield Labor councillor Sharangan Maheswaran and/or current councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in conduct including spying and blackmail towards councillor Matthew Blackmore.

These are some of the key players identified by the corruption watchdog ahead of the hearings.

World.title: Elders call for overhaul of 'tokenistic' governance on APY Lands
World.content:
A group of elders on South Australia's remote Aṉangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands say the region's current model of governance is failing — and have put forward plans for a major overhaul.

Donald Fraser, an elder from the Pukatja community, said the current model was "tokenistic, disempowering and [did] not reflect genuine self-determination for Aṉangu people".

Under his proposal, the APY Land Rights Act would be repealed and governing authority would be transferred from the executive board to an overseeing Aboriginal corporation.

Community councils based in every township across the region would become the "primary decision-makers" — a system designed to ensure local priorities were not sidelined.

But the board has rejected the plan, labelling it "absurd and totally improbable in every respect".

The call for change comes amid a tumultuous period for the APY Lands, which was placed into a three-month administration period last year.

Trent Wilkinson was appointed general manager of the APY Lands at the end of 2025. (Supplied: Facebook.)

Trent Wilkinson was appointed general manager in December, but governance was thrown back into turmoil in May, when he was purportedly sacked by the board.

Mr Wilkinson, who alleged he was the target of a conspiracy designed for financial gain, remained adamant his termination was unlawful and he still held the position.

But the board chairperson maintained he was properly removed and an interim general manager was now in charge.

Aboriginal Affairs Minister Kyam Maher said last week the government was "working with who is there at the moment", but he would not comment on the unresolved dispute.

"I'm not going to go into details about what is an employment difference of opinion and dispute between the elected APY executives and a former general manager," he said.

A 'failed system'

Under the Land Rights Act, which granted Aṉangu people ownership of their land, the region is governed by an executive board made up of 14 members — two elected from each community.

The board typically appoints the general manger, who reports to the board and is responsible for implementing resolutions and managing operations.

Mr Fraser has called for structural reform to the current governance model.

"I am speaking on behalf of many Aṉangu who are sick and tired of this failed system," he said.

"A statutory board cannot deliver self-determination. It cannot replace the authority of our elders, families, communities and homelands."

Some Aṉangu elders have put forward a new plan for governing the remote SA region. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Fraser is chairperson of the Tjilpipampa Advisory Group, which is made up of elders from every community on the APY Lands.

The group, registered as Warraritja Aboriginal Corporation, was established for provision of aged care services.

But Mr Fraser argued it was also an appropriate body to oversee governance of the region.

Under his plan, the advisory group would operate alongside individual community councils, which would be responsible for local matters.

"Each community and homeland holds deep cultural knowledge, practical solutions and lived experience," he said.

"These must sit at the centre of our governance system."

All service providers on the APY Lands would be required to report to the advisory group and community councils.

Elders Robert Stevens and Murray George, who also members of the advisory group, voiced support for abolishing the "executive model".

"They're not working with us," Mr George said.

"We've got to make the Land Rights Act go away."

The APY Lands are home to about 2,000 Aboriginal people. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Both men advocated for the establishment of community councils — a model they said was more aligned with the Pitjantjatjara Council that operated prior to the 1981 passage of the Land Rights Act.

"When we had the Pitjantjatjara Council, everything was really good … we never had any trouble" Mr George said.

"This [current] model has been really, really hard for us," Mr Stevens said.

Board, government back status quo

APY board chairperson Bernard Singer said Mr Fraser's proposal was unviable.

"The Warraritja Aboriginal Corporation is its own legal entity responsible for providing aged care services and does not have the power to govern the APY Lands," he said.

Mr Singer has defended the Land Rights Act. (ABC News: Eric Tlozek)

Mr Singer said the Land Rights Act enshrined self-determination and land rights for Aṉangu people.

"Any calls to dismantle a landmark agreement that was so hard fought for by the people of the APY Lands would extinguish self-determination and set our people back many decades," he said.

"We don't want people politically destroying one of the strongest governance models available in the nation."

A government spokeswoman said current laws ensured "decisions about APY are made by Aṉangu".

"While we acknowledge Mr Fraser's advocacy, the state government has no plans to repeal the APY Land Rights Act," she said.

World.title: Four Palestinian villagers, 2 Israeli soldiers killed in West Bank clashes
World.content:
Violence has escalated in the occupied West Bank, after clashes across the region left two Israeli soldiers and four Palestinian villagers dead on Friday.

Palestinians in the West Bank have been facing a wave of violence as Israel's hardline government, dominated by settler leaders and supporters, has overseen a surge in settlement construction in the past four years.

The international community overwhelmingly considers Israeli settlement construction in these areas to be illegal and an obstacle to peace.

Violence escalates

The Palestinian Health Ministry said Israeli soldiers shot and killed four Palestinians in the village of Tell in the northern West Bank while the military reported the deaths of two soldiers, one of whom was a settler in a local defence squad.

Two other Israelis and four more Palestinians were wounded, health officials said, and the Israeli military announced it was preparing for an "extensive" counterterror operation in the West Bank.

Father vows to fight for justice for baby killed by Israeli troops A Palestinian father promises to fight for justice for his seven-month-old son, who was shot dead by an Israeli soldier in the West Bank city of Hebron.

It said it is conducting a manhunt for Palestinians suspected of attacking Israelis and that it had apprehended two during a raid in Nablus.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a joint statement with Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, on Friday called for more troops to the West Bank and the razing of the homes of the accused in Tell, as well as collecting weapons and revoking work permits in the village.

"The security forces must be allowed to act freely and with full force against terrorism," their statement said.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich went further, saying that the villages of Tell, Iraq Burin and Beit Furik "need to look exactly like the refugee camps in Nablus and Tulkarm," referring to the mass demolition campaign that displaced tens of thousands in the West Bank towns last year.

"It is necessary to evacuate the population there for their protection and to clear these villages of terrorist infrastructure," Smotrich said.

" A sharp, determined, and unequivocal military action is required here and now. "

Human rights group B'Tselem warned the violence could spin out of control as Israeli settlers and soldiers amass near multiple Palestinian cities.

"Israeli violence is spreading across the West Bank, fuelled by Israeli politicians openly calling for revenge," said Yuli Novak, the group's executive director.

"We know where this leads. Millions of Palestinians are now completely exposed to further attacks, with no-one protecting them."

Clashes have been becoming more frequent near the West Bank city of Nablus. (AP: Majdi Mohammed)

Unclear circumstances

The exact circumstances of Friday's incident remained unclear, but Israeli media reports and interviews with local Palestinian officials suggested a group of Israeli settlers entered Tell and were confronted by residents who were fearful of an attack.

The village is off-limits to Israelis as part of Area B under the 1993 Oslo Accords struck after the first Palestinian Intifada.

According to the Israeli military, one of the villagers took one of the settlers' weapons and fired on the group, killing Benayahu Mellet, 32, a security guard in a settlement nearby.

UN report on violence against Palestinians A UN report finds that Palestinians are being subjected to "mass atrocities" by Israeli forces and being "violently repressed and controlled by the very faction that claims to govern them".

In a video of the incident, confirmed by the Israeli military and circulated online by the military correspondent for Israel's Army Radio, two armed men in civilian clothing, as well as at least one Israeli soldier, are shown pointing their weapons at a group of Palestinians who had gathered in a field.

At one point, the two armed men rushed towards several Palestinian residents with their guns drawn.

In the footage, the residents try to push them back and appear to disarm one of the men before opening fire.

In a statement, the Israeli military said it killed the man who took the settler's weapon and that he was armed when soldiers shot him.

But a separate video, published by Israeli media outlets and confirmed by the military, showed Israeli forces firing on a group of Palestinians in the same field who were already on the ground.

More than a dozen gunshots can be heard in the footage, which is less than a minute long.

The Israeli military said the suspect was one of the people killed in the field.

How Israel is strangling the Palestinian economy Palestinians argue archaeology has "become a tool, a mechanism, to justify settlement and justify the displacement of Palestinians" heritage sites along the West Bank.

It did not respond to questions about why soldiers killed the other men — all of whom were related — or how long after the original altercation the killings took place.

Later, Israeli army chief Eyal Zamir said he was sending more troops to the occupied West Bank.

Yossi Dagan, head of the Samaria Regional Council, a settler group in the northern West Bank, posted a video online in the wake of the Tell confrontation demanding the government crack down hard on Palestinians.

"We demand an iron fist and for the government to carry out a wide military operation against the Palestinian Authority and against Hamas," he said.

Confrontation more frequent

Five Palestinian villages surrounding Nablus were attacked by Israeli settlers on Friday, according to the Palestinian news agency WAFA.

The towns and villages surrounding Nablus sit in one of the most violent parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

In addition to newly approved settlements, at least nine farming outposts dot the area and attacks by Israeli settlers, army incursions and confrontations have become frequent.

Prospects for Palestinian statehood 'disappearing' The two former world leaders are demanding the international community heap more pressure on Israel to change course.

Palestinians and human rights groups have increasingly documented armed settlers entering villages in the area.

Livestock theft, arson and the defacement of mosques are routinely reported.

According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, since the beginning of this year, 87 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank governorates, including 21 by Israeli settlers.

Israeli deaths have repeatedly been followed by revenge against nearby Palestinian communities called "price tag" attacks.

That pattern followed the March 21 death of 18-year-old Yehuda Sherman, who was killed when a Palestinian vehicle struck his ATV near Beit Imrin. Senior politicians, including Smotrich, attended Sherman's funeral and called for vengeance.

At the time, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented 32 settler attacks affecting 30 Palestinian villages and communities across the West Bank, about a third near the Nablus governorate over the following two days.

Settlers torched homes and vehicles, vandalised property and assaulted residents, injuring at least 32 Palestinians, according to OCHA.

More than 700,000 Israelis live in the occupied West Bank and east Jerusalem, territories captured by Israel in 1967 and sought by the Palestinians for an independent state along with the Gaza Strip.

World.title: 'Game-changer': Tracking collars help monitor vulnerable koala populations
World.content:
Thermal drones and innovative tracking collars are a "game-changer" for researchers who are addressing declining koala populations across south-east Queensland.

Using the technology, they can detect multiple koalas in a day and respond sooner if the animal is sick or injured.

"We get up early in the morning when there's really good differential between the cool forest and the koalas' heat, and the thermal camera on the drone just glows if you happen to fly over a koala," University of Queensland researcher Dr Sean FitzGibbon said.

It's a far cry from how they used to find koalas, just eight years ago.

Loading...

"We would go out spotlighting at night with torches looking for eye shine and we would spend days fanned out in a line walking through the bush, tediously looking up trying to spot one," Dr FitzGibbon said.

" This is way more efficient and means we can get a lot more done. "

Researchers use an app to monitor the locations of koalas in real-time. (Supplied)

Innovative tracking collars are also helping to boost conservation efforts because it allows researchers to monitor the movements of koalas in real-time.

The solar-powered, remote system weighs just 20 grams and provides location data which is sent to a mobile phone about four times a day.

"It's an important advancement in animal welfare … a few times it's saved koalas lives where we found a sick koala that might've died in a few days if we hadn't responded to the GPS signal," Dr FitzGibbon said.

Technology helps koala repopulation program

The technology is being used to monitor koalas across south-east Queensland but has been particularly effective in the Brisbane Koala Bushlands at Burbank, where a program is underway to address the declining population.

The field-based research program aims to treat sick koalas one-by-one, while supplementing the current population with healthy youngsters.

Veterinarian Dr Amber Gillett is part of a program to boost koala numbers at Burbank, in Brisbane's south-east. (ABC News: Liz Gwynn)

"We need to act quickly in terms of removing diseased animals, treating what we can and then helping with new genetics and new animals to come in as breeding animals," UQ research fellow and veterinarian Dr Amber Gillett said.

" We're now trying to bring it full circle because we've seen the population crash and we are hoping it will climb again. "

Researchers release healthy koalas wearing innovative tracking collars so their movements can be monitored daily on an app. (ABC News: Liz Gwynn)

Deliah, is among several young koalas that have been relocated after she was rescued from the Whites Hill Reserve area in Brisbane.

"They come in for various reasons but almost always they are sub-adult koalas that are trying to find new habitat," Dr FitzGibbon said.

"So then those little ones cross roads, walk into backyards with dogs or trip into swimming pools … we've had all of those types of koalas rescued and released at this site."

A major project is underway to bring back the koala population in the Burbank bushland which has suffered massive losses in the past 20-30 years. (ABC News: Liz Gwynn)

Portable vet clinic

Chlamydia is the biggest threat to koalas at Burbank, which is why every koala found is examined and treated, while briefly anaesthetised, to determine whether the animal can be released back into the wild or whether it needs to go into care.

This is all done on site, thanks to a retrofitted caravan which acts as a portable vet clinic.

Dr Gillett assesses and treats koalas in a mobile vet clinic. (ABC News: Liz Gwynn)

"I can do bloods, I've got a microscope, I've got blood spinners which means I can do all of that in the field, so I have a really good handle on what's going on with the koala," Dr Gillett said.

"That reduces stress on the koala and reduces the impact on the wildlife hospitals that are always really busy."

Chlamydia is the biggest threat to koalas at Burbank. (ABC News: Liz Gwynn)

The program, which is a collaboration with the Brisbane City Council, the Queensland government, wildlife rescue groups and animal hospitals, has been running for 18 months and has already led to the birth of two joeys.

"It's like almost giving birth to my own child in some ways, you are responsible for bringing that animal in and then you see that result," Dr Gillett said.

"We bring in the right animals and we give them the environment and they can do it themselves, they will bolster their own population."

World.title: Worker housing for $1.5b Queensland wind farm faces opposition
World.content:
James Barclay has been studying the sky for the best part of seven decades.

But the 79-year-old astronomer says a temporary workers' camp proposed to be built next door would put his observatory in the Queensland town of Kingaroy at risk of closure.

"If this camp goes ahead, the lighting alone will be enough to close this observatory down," Dr Barclay said.

UK-based energy company Renewable Energy Systems (RES) plans to build temporary housing for up to 424 workers for the construction of its proposed Tarong West Wind Farm near the small town of Kumbia.

The accommodation is proposed for land near Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen Airport outside Kingaroy. (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

Construction on the $1.5 billion project is expected to begin later this year after it received approval by the federal government.

Once complete, it could produce enough energy to power 230,000 homes annually.

The proposed camp needed to house the workers is yet to be approved by the South Burnett Regional Council.

While the accommodation would be a $68 million investment in the town, many Kingaroy residents have voiced opposition to the project.

Camp in wrong area, residents say

The opponents, including Dr Barclay, have said the proposed accommodation, about 40 kilometres from the wind farm, was too far from the project and the area was zoned for community facilities.

(From left) Karen Bjelke-Petersen, Grant Arrell and Helen Greenslade oppose the proposed camp location. (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

Neighbouring resident Grant Arell built his home 15 years ago, and his property boundary would sit about 110 metres from the proposed accommodation.

Mr Arrell said he never expected to be next to a large accommodation facility and agreed it should be built closer to the wind farm.

"It's not what we signed up for," he said.

" The reality is, I think, the vast majority of the community are not against sensible development and sensible progress. But the progress has to make sense, the progress needs to be in the right areas. "

The proposed camp will be made up of 106 four-bedroom demountable accommodation units, an industrial canteen, a gym, a recreation room, an administration building and enough car parking for every worker.

The proposed camp would feature 106 four-bedroom units, communal facilities and parking for more than 400 vehicles. (Supplied: South Burnett Regional Council)

The South Burnett Regional Council said developer RES initially investigated sites closer to the wind farm, but issues with water supply and road suitability led the council to suggest the aerodrome site in its discussions last year.

"Council's objective in this offer was to ease the burden on and concerns of the Kumbia community," a spokesperson said.

In its application to the council, RES said while the proposal did not fit within current zoning for community use, the legacy infrastructure like plumbing and car parking would make the development appropriate.

The site of the proposed temporary workers camp is being used by a community organisation to grow wheat. (ABC Southern Qld: Dan McCray)

Opposition despite investment

While most of the $68 million investment would go towards housing, RES said $20 million would flow to local businesses during the life of the accommodation project.

The company said housing was limited across the region with only about 100 rooms available to workers during the proposed construction.

RES said it would use existing accommodation, but significantly more was needed.

"Significant additional capacity is still required," an RES spokesperson said.

Community members have until August 7 to provide feedback on the proposal. (Supplied: Grant Arrell)

South Burnett Regional Council said in a statement that the application was being assessed while in the public notification phase, with residents invited to lodge submissions up to the August 7 deadline.

It said all accommodation would be removed once the wind farm was built.

Despite this, Karen Bjelke-Petersen, who runs accommodation nearby, said she feared the development could affect the area's appeal.

"People come here for the quiet," she said.

"Whether I lived close or not, I can't see any advantage to it being here."

For Dr Barclay, the fight was far from over.

"While I've got two legs in the vertical, I won't go away," he said.

World.title: How Hani harnessed mum and mana to go 'balls out' for bronze
World.content:
There is a two-minute countdown clock when para powerlifters enter the arena.

In that time they have to settle on the bench, most get their legs strapped down, align their back and shoulders under the bar, get their grip perfect, then lift.

Eventually, the pump-up music fades out when the lifter is finally ready, usually about halfway through the time.

Not Australia's Hani Watson, though.

For the first 30-40 seconds of her time on the bench, Watson, an effusive and effervescent athlete who loves a chat, takes a moment of supreme stillness.

As trusted coach Simon Bergner hurriedly organises straps and chalk with arena staff, he at no point rushes his charge.

As the crowd nervously watches the seconds tick down, Watson sits, eyes closed, breath steady, mind awash with the words of her late mum.

"You got this darlin'."

Hani Watson manages rogue bones and a body on fire When Hani Watson settles under the barbell at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, she will be lifting more than just the plates on the bar.

Watson credits mother Laurita June "Bub" Rayward, who died in 2023, for "creating the strong woman" she has become.

"I believe in having that spirit, that energy, that mana, my culture that's within me, the Australian spirit and just sitting there and calming myself down and listening to that internal voice," she said after winning a second straight women's heavyweight Commonwealth Games bronze medal.

"As kids we don't listen to our parents, but I'm listening to them now. And they told me, 'This is your superpower, this is what you can do, this is what you need to focus on.'"

She was plenty strong enough in 2022 to win bronze with a best lift of 127 kilograms, and shattered that number with a final re-rack of 147kg in Glasgow on Saturday morning AEST.

"I didn't actually think I was going to hit the numbers coach was gonna ask me to hit," she said.

"But I just blocked it out, I didn't wanna know. I just went balls out and just hit it."

A "wild" crowd at Glasgow's Armadillo was enraptured by the ease with which she completed her lifts — although the third took some shifting.

But the loudest moments were reserved for the Nigerians, who collected silver through Rita Ferdinard and gold courtesy of the all-conquering Folashade Oluwafemiayo, who shattered the 86kg+ world record with a final lift of 175kg for a second straight Commonwealth gold.

Folashade Oluwafemiayo (centre) is seemingly untouchable, but Watson is chasing. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Watson is chasing her, and is hoping to have closed the gap by the time the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics roll around.

"It's nice to have someone to chase and I keep chasing her, I keep looking up to her," she said.

"I think it's important to have mentors in the game. She's been doing it since she was a teenager so she's got a lot of years on me — maybe about 30 years in the game — and I've been doing it for five, so I've got a lot to learn from her."

Oluwafemiayo also broke her own Games record score of 134.8 points despite weighing 15kg less than Watson (Commonwealth Games scores are calculated by comparing body weight to weight on the bar).

Swimmers spark medal rush on day one Lani Pallister wins Australia's first gold of these Commonwealth Games in the women's 400m freestyle, with more Aussies scooping up medals in the pool on the first full day of competition.

Both athletes had added 20kg of apparently pure muscle since Birmingham.

"Every time I see her it's like she's become this big chunky cow that she's eaten or something. It's muscle upon muscle on that woman," Watson said with pure admiration.

"I just watch her in awe. I ask her what's changed, what do you bench, what are you eating, and she tells me everything.

"I need someone to look up to because the sport's always changing, the goalposts are always changing.

"As long as she's there I've gotta keep watching her and she's watching me too. She knows I'm on her tail."

World.title: Gold, bronze and $30,000 in 50 minutes: The unexpected star of Australia’s big night in the pool
World.content:
SportSwimmingCommonwealth Games Gold, bronze and $30,000 in 50 minutes: The unexpected star of Australia’s big night in the pool Billie Eder July 25, 2026 — 7:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scroll down to see the medal tally after day one of the Commonwealth Games. Glasgow: Jenna Forrester wasn’t meant to swim in the women’s 200-metre backstroke at these Commonwealth Games. She originally missed out on a spot in the event after placing fourth at the Australian trials last month, and was given the late call-up when reigning champion Kaylee McKeown had to withdraw with glandular fever. Jenna Forrester shocked the field to win gold in the women’s 200m backstroke. Getty Images And yet, on Saturday morning (AEST) she found herself with a gold medal around her neck after stunning the field with a 2:08.17 swim – her second medal of the night after claiming bronze in the 400m freestyle just 50 minutes earlier.



“I did not expect that to happen tonight. I’m so over the moon,” Forrester said. “I didn’t really have much expectation going into the 400m free or the 200m backstroke, so I’m really happy with how that went ... I really just went into tonight with a positive attitude, and I felt like I had nothing to lose.” McKeown has dominated the event at every major meet since the Tokyo Olympics. The only time Forrester had raced internationally in the 200m backstroke was at the world championships in 2023, when she finished 10th. After tossing up whether she should start at all, given she thought she had a better chance in the 400m earlier in the night, she was ecstatic she had decided to go for it.



“I wasn’t sure if I was going to do the 200m backstroke because I thought I had a better shot at the 400m freestyle. But I spoke to my coach, and we just thought it’s a great opportunity,” Forrester said. “And I felt like I couldn’t turn down a swim at the Commonwealth Games because that’s pretty awesome. So yeah, I decided to do it, and I’m over the moon.” Jenna Forrester after realising she had won gold. AP Photo/Kin Cheung It was a sensational finish from Forrester, who was all the way back in fifth at the halfway point of the race – a position that had only improved to fourth by time she made the turn for the final 50m. “I spoke to my coach [Dean Boxall], and he said I had a very even split, and a lot of people said ‘you were really far behind at the 100m turn’,” Forrester said.



“I wasn’t really sure where I was in the field, but at the 100m mark I did have a sneaky look, and I was like ‘wow, I am really far behind’. But, I know the back end, especially in the 200m backstroke, is my strength as I am a 400m medley swimmer. “So that endurance work really comes in handy. It’s more seeing if I can catch up. I don’t always, but tonight I managed to.” Forrester is also now $30,000 richer because of Hancock Prospecting’s medal bonuses for Australian swimmers – $20,000 for winning gold and $10,000 for bronze. Her mother Louisa, who fought cancer two years ago, wasn’t poolside on Friday night. She was racing an ultra-marathon in Kyrgyzstan, but Forrester said that was who she got her fighting spirit from.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Aussie star says she was scared to reveal her Jewish identity at the Olympics. Now she’s found her voice again “She’s definitely the toughest person I know, and she’s probably my No.1 inspiration,” Forrester said. “To have a mother like that, even though she’s really tough herself, she is only ever supportive towards me, and I always know that no matter what my result is, she’ll always be proud of me.” Forrester still has the 200m and 400m individual medley to come, and said she’s setting her sights high after her results on day one. “I think I just need to approach the rest of my swims with the same mentality,” she said.
