World.title: Mutiny on the golf course: Why members are threatening legal action against billionaire’s son
World.content:
NationalNSWInvestigation Mutiny on the golf course: Why members are threatening legal action against billionaire’s son Lucy Macken Updated July 25, 2026 — 7:03am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If Felix Ming Ze Lee, the 25-year-old son of beleaguered billionaire businessman Phillip Dong Fang Lee, is wondering what else could go wrong this week, members of the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club have bad news. As former Victorian premier Dan Andrews checked out the championship course earlier this week, more than 100 members of the privately owned, Lee-family controlled championship golf club have threatened legal action against the management amid claims of oppressive conduct and excessive annual subscription fee rises that they say are in breach of the club’s constitution. Former Victorian premier Dan Andrews checked out the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club this week. Artwork: Monqiue Westermann Fuelling heightened animosity among some members are falling resale values of membership shareholdings, and new joining, administration and registration fees, prompting members to describe it as now the only decent golf club in Sydney with a “waiting list of sellers”. The mutiny of members from the prestigious course caps off a tumultuous week for the young businessman. It started with dinner with the prime minister, only to be overshadowed days later by revelations about damning allegations from the tax office about his father’s “sham” financial arrangements to funnel huge sums of money from China to Australia.



An exhaustive investigation into the financial affairs of Phillip Lee has not only shed new light on the previously opaque origins of his wealth, but also included suspicions that the family patriarch continued operating his businesses in China decades after he told Australian authorities he had sold his business assets in China. “The [tax] commissioner believes that Mr Lee still has business and financial interest in the PRC [People’s Republic of China], notwithstanding his previous representations to the Australian government as part of his application for migration that all of his businesses in the PRC were sold,” states the tax office affidavit. Further, “those businesses appear to be held in structures which mask Mr Lee’s true ownership and control of those assets. In particular, the commissioner believes that Mr Lee has structured his financial affairs in such a way as to give the appearance that his mother and business associates are the owners of businesses which are in truth operated and owned by him”. More than 100 members of the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club have sent a legal letter of demand to the Lee family management. Wolter Peeters Felix Lee has sought to distance himself from his father’s business and financial affairs in recent years, founding the Lee Family Office, and inviting former federal treasurer and ex-ambassador to the United States Joe Hockey on as chairman.



Felix Lee declined to comment in response to questions about the tax office’s damning allegations about his father. “Phillip Lee’s tax affairs are his own and are not related to Felix Lee,” a spokesperson said on his behalf earlier this week. In response to inquiries about the legal letter, a spokesman for the club’s management said both parties are communicating in relation to their clients’ respective asserted, but contested, positions. Felix Lee’s week started with dinner with the prime minister and ended with a mutiny from members of his Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club. “The board has received legal correspondence, has considered the allegations carefully, and through its legal representatives has responded comprehensively, rejecting the allegations made,” the spokesperson said. “The company maintains that it has acted lawfully, in accordance with the club’s Constitution and its directors’ duties.” Central to Felix Lee’s responsibilities in recent years has been the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club, a prestigious championship course purchased by his parents from a syndicate of Japanese investors a decade ago.



Felix Lee was appointed director in November 2020, a few weeks after his 20th birthday, and more recently elevated to chairman. Fellow board members include his uncle Victor Lin, known among members as a passionate golfer, and Felix’s younger brother Edward Feng Zhao Lee, who was appointed early last year soon after his 19th birthday. Felix’s mother, Xiaobei Shi, stepped down early last year. Related Article Investigation The 25-year-old tasked with fixing billionaire father’s mess enlists help of Joe Hockey Former club member George Kalil didn’t know who Felix was when he first met him at a committee meeting at the club in about 2023, but he hasn’t forgotten it. “Felix Lee came in, unintroduced and totally unknown to me and other committee members,” Kalil said. “I thought he was there to take the coffee order, but he wasn’t the new waiter. He was Phillip Lee’s son, and he just launched into a tirade saying ‘you guys have to know your place’.” As Kalil and others understood it, things were set for a shake-up at the club. Among the changes, a member-elected committee was abolished three years ago and replaced with an advisory panel appointed by the Lee family directors.



While the original committee structure ostensibly allowed members some oversight of the club’s financial governance, the new advisory panel did not, according to members. Related Article Exclusive

Political donations Revealed: What really happened at the PM’s secretive Point Piper dinner A spokesman for the board said it believes the current structure improves effective member engagement because it has invited a more diverse cross-section of the membership base, including women, those with different playing skills and members who previously did not feel their views were being heard. When the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club opened in late 1993 it was the first championship course built in Sydney in two decades. Wolter Peeters The members’ letter claims annual subscription fees have risen well beyond what they claim is the club’s constitution’s mandated cap of 5 per cent a year to total more than 20 per cent in the past two years.



The board rejected the claims of a constitution cap of 5 per cent on annual fees and said it wasn’t responsible for changes in membership resale values. “Subscriptions are determined depending upon working capital and expenditure of the club from time to time.” Claims from the membership that the board has imposed new member joining fee, administration fee and registration fee when a member tries to sell and transfer their shares were also rejected by the board, instead stating that the joining and administration fees have been in place since about 2000. In correspondence seen by this masthead, a founding member was revealed to have waited a year with no buyers before he recently sold his membership for $12,000, less than the club’s new joining fee of $12,500. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations ‘Sham’ loans, ‘unexplained’ wealth: Albanese dinner donor’s $260m family tax fight revealed One of the members who is currently on a waiting list to sell their stake in the club is James de Stigter, who paid about $45,000 to join. After injury left him unable to play for the past 18 months, he put his membership up for sale and expects it to sell for about $9000.



After Stephen Schinagel’s wife Heather Mead died, he made inquiries about putting her membership up for sale and was told late last year they were selling for about $20,000. It was a dramatic loss on the $65,000 she paid in 2017. It has since been discounted to $15,000 in a bid to hasten the process. “The market value of memberships is influenced by a range of factors, including broader economic conditions, discretionary spending, and market demand, and risks associated with membership were well documented in the several company prospectuses,” the spokesperson said. Members were hoping to flag their concerns at the annual general meeting held June 30, in particular about why annual fees increased given a $7.2 million cash reserve held by the club, but the opportunity never arose. Having opened the meeting, Felix Lee promptly announced there would be no dividend declared, and closed the meeting. Two minutes later, it was all over. World.title: Old blokes might win stuff, but Australia sideline youth at their peril
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Opinion Old blokes might win stuff, but Australia sideline youth at their peril Daniel Brettig The Age chief cricket writer July 25, 2026 — 7:00am

July 25, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Old blokes win stuff” was a phrase beloved of all-rounder and now coach Dan Christian, as he spent his final few playing years hoovering up Twenty20 franchise trophies around the world. It’s also a neat summary of the philosophy followed by the national selectors, as they do all they can to keep the ageing core of the Australian Test team together for a glut of major assignments over the next 12 months. Still together after all these years: Australian bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins in 2018. AP When selection chair George Bailey, coach Andrew McDonald and selector Tony Dodemaide got together in 2022, they agreed on an approach that marked a significant departure from previous panels. Rather than playing their best team whenever possible, the focus was narrowed to major events. Test series and World Cups were king, while bilateral white-ball series fell a long way down the order of preference. They have effectively become proving grounds for young players, as well as contractual obligations for Cricket Australia.



The Test match focus on the now was enhanced by the aim of securing a spot in the world championship final every two years, adding context to lower-profile series dotted in between bouts against England and India. By rationing resources, they hoped to extend the careers of great players. Editor's pick Australian cricket Final frontier: Smith and ageing Test team vow to complete unfinished business away from home Four years on, however, a two-match series against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay seems an odd juncture at which to roll out Steve Smith, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Scott Boland and Nathan Lyon, all of whom are now 35 and older. There are sensible arguments for reconvening the frontline Test team ahead of 12 unrelenting months of series against South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. But the prospect of playing an XI with only one player under the age of 30, against a Bangladesh side that just lost a Test by an innings to Zimbabwe, is an unsettling one. The flipside of Australia’s approach over the past four years has been that opportunities for younger players are only provided when there is an injury or an obvious gap in the side.



That has meant the likes of Sam Konstas, Nathan McSweeney and Todd Murphy have been exposed to Test cricket in the toughest circumstances: against a rampaging Jasprit Bumrah, in the crucible of an Ashes series in England, or on uneven Caribbean pitches against Shamar Joseph. Those experiences were bruising ones for the trio, more so for being followed by omission from the team. It would have been useful to see any one of these players granted the opportunity to impose themselves on Bangladesh. After all, a Travis Head blitz is not going to prove much the selectors don’t already know, nor will a brace of hundreds by Smith do much more than pad out his formidable Test record. Numerous senior figures in the game spoken to by this masthead expressed surprise at the absence of even one young batter from the squad. Konstas and Ollie Peake were both mentioned by several as ideal candidates to play. The 13 chosen this week will likely be augmented by other non-playing squad members around the two Tests, but their exposure will be limited to training sessions. Jasprit Bumrah gets Nathan McSweeney for a duck in Perth in 2024. Getty Images As it is, Jake Weatherald, Cameron Green and Marnus Labuschagne will be the trio most eager to find runs and confidence in Darwin and Mackay, having offered only glimpses of their best in last summer’s Ashes series. Weatherald’s chemistry with Head is obvious, but Test cricket is a game of performance rather than a rom com.



A more persuasive argument for playing an old team against Bangladesh comes in the form of using the series as a quasi-fitness test. Hazlewood, Cummins and Lyon in particular need to reassure the selectors of their ability to stay on the park, making the Top-End Tests a useful juncture to do so before the South Africa tour. While Cummins’ back stress injury may ultimately work in favour of longevity, meaning he has more Test matches to play over the next three years or so, Hazlewood and Lyon are facing stiffer questions of durability. Editor's pick Australian cricket Why Australia’s next Test opponents are in crisis mode Hazlewood has now pulled up lame in his first long-form game back from injury too many times for comfort, while Lyon’s soft-tissue problems should at the very least necessitate he is moved away from outfield duty and remoulded, Jimmy Anderson style, into a close catcher. In the meantime, CA have an invitational XI going north to play Bangladesh in their warm-up fixture. Another group is heading to Chennai for the annual visit to the MRF Academy in India. Australia A tour India later in the year. Numerous white ball players may travel there, rather than playing in concurrent limited overs series against South Africa and Zimbabwe.



Apart from Konstas, Peake, Cooper Connolly and Campbell Kellaway, Australia also have an emerging generation of fast bowlers currently navigating the same kinds of injuries once traversed by Cummins and company. In years to come, the likes of Callum Vidler and Mahli Beardman will get the chance to make their mark. There is still hope for Lance Morris and Jhye Richardson, too. For now, the selectors continue to err on the side of experience, even for an opponent as modest as Bangladesh. History will be the judge of whether they have pulled the right rein. Nathan Lyon - 38 years old

Steve Smith - 37

Scott Boland - 37

Josh Hazlewood - 35

Alex Carey - 34

Pat Cummins - 33

Travis Head - 32

Beau Webster - 32

Jake Weatherald - 31

World.title: Beefed-up brekkie rolls to golden boreks: Sydney’s best cafes with exceptional food
World.content:
Eating outEssential cafes and bakeries Beefed-up brekkie rolls to golden boreks: Sydney’s best cafes with exceptional food The commitment to detail and sheer deliciousness of every dish make these cafes really stand out. All hail the very best cafe food of 2026. Good Food Guide reviewers July 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cafe food has long been associated with simplicity and speed. Granola with a scoop of Greek yoghurt, fried eggs, a chicken sandwich to-go. If you didn’t know any better, you might think it’s the same deal at cafes like Serva in Seaforth, Ellenin Alexandria or Angus in Marrickville. What’s the big deal about a cheese toastie, after all? Well, maybe you haven’t tried Serva’s: filled with maple-glazed mushrooms, house made mushroom XO sauce, kombu butter and three types of cheese, with a side of syrupy thick blueberry chutney (also made in-house). It’s delicious, textural and entirely singular in Sydney. This list is part of the 100 Essential Sydney Cafes and Bakeries of 2026, a celebration of the cafes with that kind of exceptional attention to detail, from a fish sandwich at Angus that takes three days to make, to a slice of sourdough toast with snapper pate and pickled fennel at Sway in Manly (everything made from scratch). Angus’ brekkie roll with corned beef, cheddar and house relish is also worth a look. Dion Georgopoulos Angus



Angus is the sleeper hit of Marrickville cafes. It launched quietly as Agnes in 2023, then gradually changed its name, ownership and opening hours. The menu kept improving, strengthened by ties to cult-favourite Kirrawee bakery Thoroughbread and a commitment to deceptively labour-intense dishes. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Did you know that making their bestselling crumbed fish sandwich requires three days of steaming fish, creating stock, making sauce and baking bread? That they cure the salmon to make gravlax for their Scandi-style brekkie plate? Or that they poach the rhubarb for each rhubarb matcha matte? No wonder it’s getting tough to score a table. 69 Meeks Road, Marrickville, angusmarrickville.com.au Co-owner Jovan Radevski stocks the cabinet at Burek Brothers. Sitthixay Ditthavong Burek Brothers



It’s one of the most underrated snacks in Sydney: a single, handheld slice of filo pastry pie filled with fresh ricotta and feta cheese, or maybe a lightly spiced mixture of minced beef and caramelised onion, and then baked until golden. Some call it borek, but brothers Nikola and Jovan Radevski use its Balkan name, burek, and each morning they draw upon their Macedonian great-grandfather’s 100-year-old recipe to make seven savoury and sweet varieties from scratch, using dairy from Vannella, and meat from Lebanese butcher The Butcher Boys in Rockdale. 162 Bay Street, Rockdale, burekbrothers.com.au Dogs and humans enjoying the Cafe Cressida courtyard. Jennifer Soo Cafe Cressida



Chef Phil Wood and Lis Davies are the couple behind Cressida, which is named after their daughter and is fundamentally a nice place to drink coffee and read the paper. Cushioned seats are upholstered in marigold stripes, water is poured in Maison Balzac glasses and illustrations of a prancing burger decorate the exterior walls. The real-life cheeseburger is a fun time too, featuring a beefy medium-rare patty on a squishy potato bun. Fresh produce is a cut-above across the board and the kitchen will send out a terrific version of eggs any way you like them with Iggy’s sourdough. Later, enjoy that same crusty sourdough with Charentes-Poitou butter, oysters and champagne in the courtyard, which is what life is all about at the end of the day. Must order: The Sicilian-style orange cake made famous by Margie Agostini when she ran her own cafe at the site in the 90s. 118 Queen Street, Woollahra, cafecressida.com.au Cafe Lewi



It took three years for fine-dining chefs John and Leva Laureti to transform a suburban corner store into the elegant cafe of their dreams. People wander in from the street, lured by a counter display of desserts – none so beautiful as the miniature marjolaine, frosted with the flourish of a vintage wedding cake. The brunch menu convinces them to stay, making the tough call between salmon confit on a crunchy potato base with whipped avo, or the abundantly yolky, teriyaki breakfast bun. This one was worth the wait. Good to know: Dinner service has started on Wednesday and Friday nights, the former dedicated to steak frites. 8A Victoria Street, Lewisham, cafelewi.com.au Cafe Monaka



Look around at the tables at Cafe Monaka and you’ll notice everyone has ordered the same thing: a plump pink cutlet of shio-koji marinated salmon, rolled tamagoyaki egg omelette, soy-simmered green beans and a bowl of miso soup. It’s the asagohan, a well-portioned Japanese breakfast plate built on the ichiju-sansai principle of “one soup, three dishes”. Green tea is the traditional accompaniment, and Cafe Monaka imports its sencha, matcha and hojicha straight from Japan. 2/24 Waratah Street, Mona Vale, cafemonaka.com.au Cafe Baby Finger Two blocks from Parramatta Road, the mood is serene at Baby Finger, with simple decor and a cooling through-breeze. Owner-chef John Jeong welcomes every customer with a lilting “Helloo” and a menu that – from glazed French toast ladled with plump strawberry coulis, citrus mascarpone and macerated balsamic berries to fried eggplant and charred bush tomato curry topped with a poached egg – is not usual cafe fare.



Jeong also bakes his own focaccia, sourdough and brioche, and is the kind of accommodating guy who will still make scrambled eggs if you ask for it. Good to know: Cafe Baby Finger (named after Jeong’s habit of taking photos accidentally featuring his little finger) is also a top destination for anyone with a pram. Unit 27/12 Layton Street, Camperdown The pork banh mi at Ca Phe Mai Parker Blain Ca Phe Mai



From banh mi filled with bacon and soft steamed egg, to brekkie muffins served with lemongrass pork sausage patties, Ca Phe Mai combines Vietnamese flavours with Australian cafe favourites to create a menu unlike anywhere else in Sydney. The ca phe muoi (Single O espresso sweetened with condensed milk and thick, salted coconut cream) is dangerously good with a thick slice of toasted banana bread, spread with Vietnamese coffee butter, but chicken broth dishes like pho ga and laksa are the real must-tries, made with a 40-year-old secret family recipe. Good to know: This is a day-to-night venue, transforming into a wine bar after dark. 377 New South Head Road (enter via Kiaora Lane), Double Bay, caphemai.com.au Yu Ozone and her husband Masa at Comeco. Edwina Pickles



Comeco Foods This organic Japanese cafe will change how you think about gluten-free and plant-based food. Stop by for a matcha latte sweetened with house made strawberry puree, or one of those revelatory “sourdoughnuts”, filled and fried to order. Nourishment is the express goal here, and it’s done with deceptive deliciousness – who would have known the katsu curry roux is made with 11 vegetables if it weren’t on the menu? Try a bite of (almost) everything with the tempura and onigiri plate, then return at dinnertime for the colourful sushi platter that might include grilled capsicum nigiri and aburi eggplant rolls. Good to know: The new dinner service features specialty Japanese alcohol like yuzushu, available by the glass. 524A King Street, Newtown, comecofoods.com.au



The famous fish burger at Ellen. Ellen It’s difficult to make muesli exciting, but at Ellen it’s a textural delight of puffed rice, yoghurt and crunch, served with pistachio cream and fresh strawberries. It’s that kind of commitment to the small things which makes this place special. It recently became the go-to for fish burgers in Sydney – they’re generously portioned, carefully wrapped and full of acidity and heat from pickles and seeded mustard. But that’s only the start – the kitchen goes beyond typical cafe fare with specials like poached Queensland grouper, served with fish bone broth, chives and a paper-thin slice of pancetta. Good to know: About half of the seating is outside (and dog-friendly) – lovely on a sunny day, less so when it rains.



Unit 153/18 Huntley Street, Alexandria Haven, Rosebery. Haven Specialty Coffee Whichever of Haven’s five locations you visit, expect Scandi-minamilist lines and a menu that squeezes hits into every square inch. Owners Kit Tran and Herman Chiu roast coffee beans in house, and all the staples are present and correct, but next-wave drinkers can expect the lychee coconut water under cold matcha foam or cold brew topped with peach-infused cream to hit the spot. Food? Pandan-coconut French toast and Mont Blanc cake are standouts on an inventive Asian-inspired brunch menu.



Must order: Chilli scramble with roasted peanuts. 7 Crewe Place, Rosebery, havencoffee.com.au The new kaisendon filled with fresh quality seafood at Kurumac. Kurumac Owners Eugene Leung and Dika Brianata’s Marrickville cafe Kurumac set a new standard for Japanese cafe fare in 2019, but the menu revamp in July took it to another level of authenticity and innovation.



In the morning, go for a soft egg sando with curry mayo on fluffy shokupan bread from nearby Azuki bakery. For a lunch that’s substantial, yet balanced, try the teishoku set, featuring a soft omelette spiked with salty mentaiko (pollock roe), grilled salmon, slices of poached chicken, clam miso soup, pickled daikon, sauteed spinach and rice. House special drinks include the hoji-sso, where an iced hojicha latte is combined with black sugar and topped with espresso cream. 107 Addison Road, Marrickville, kurumac.com Pina Don’t be deterred by the ever-present queues crowding the laneway – Pina is worth the wait. Service remains friendly under pressure, moving efficiently through the cafe’s blushed industrial interiors to deliver a vast menu of classic brunch fare, made better.



Sourdough pancakes become supersized, with sweet or savoury toppings to choose from; a massive, crisp potato rosti is piled with chunks of cucumber and herb-flecked creme fraiche. And it’s all adaptable, with more than 15 sides, spanning haloumi to kimchi. Good to know: Pina is licensed, with a short selection of Australian wines. All of the condiments are made in house at Serva. Dylan Coker Serva Serva, a bright orange cafe in the Northern Beaches, is where owner-chef Miles Ackermans shows off his vast range of pickles and preserves – sold retail, or served in sandwiches, toasties, muffins and salads.



Join his growing group of customers-turned-mates, and start swooning over umami-rich mushroom toasties, laced with kombu butter and served with zucchini pickle; and marvelling at the meaty, crunchy, melty Reuben with apple and celery kraut. A Freshwater location has been announced to open sometime in winter 2026, too. Good to know: Need a last-minute birthday gift? Pick up a pickle jar and locally crafted ceramics here. Suite 1/538 Sydney Road, Seaforth, servasyd.com.au SIT in Marrickville. Dion Georgopoulos SIT



First, there was Baba’s Place: a hatted Marrickville restaurant where Eastern Europe meets Western Sydney. Now, from the same team, there is SIT: a cafe with intentional eclecticism and Mediterranean-ish food, like Baba’s well-travelled grandchild with a penchant for freddo espressos. There are two absolute must-tries: the pot-set yoghurt with honey and walnuts, and the pancakes. The former is a textural joy so delicious you’ll question everything you knew about yoghurt; the latter, a perfectly cooked vehicle for maple syrup and a paper-thin sheet of butter that slowly, theatrically, melts in. 387 Illawarra Road, Marrickville, comesit.com.au Even the sourdough bread is made from scratch at Sway. Dion Georgopoulos Sway Manly



Sway has a warmth that extends from the sunlit footpath to the service. Look beyond the car park views to a menu that evokes the spirit of Manly: a bright take on Aussie brunch, lush with salads and hearty with house-made sourdough, each dish deeply considered. Take the honey-roasted pear and seed porridge, painted with blueberry and orange blossom compote, or the light pâté made of local snapper, creme fraiche and dill, slathered thickly on toast with lemony fennel salad. The specialty coffee is notably good, but the peach and Earl Grey iced tea can’t be beaten. Shop C, 1/13 The Corso, Manly Taguan Cafe Taguan promises a “home away from home” for the Filipino diaspora, but everyone’s welcome. In November, the cafe moved into a two-storey terrace with a cheerfully lived-in feel – mementos on the walls, golden pothos trailing the ceiling, trays of warm pandesal rolls lining the counter.



Brunch here blends tradition, innovation and fun: toasties pull apart in streaks of purple ube halaya and molten cheese; queso fundido, warm in the iron skillet, leans into richness with crumbled longganisa sausage; and pork adobo, from a family recipe, is the comforting signature dish, tart and tender, on a bed of garlic rice. Good to know: The ube matcha might be the most expensive drink, but it’s worth every dollar. 274 Abercrombie Street, Darlington Tento specialises in ramen and ochazuke. TenTo



The courtyard restaurant-cafe is hemmed in by concrete and humming with morning energy, steam rolling off hand-built clay bowls of rich tonkotsu ramen and salmon ochazuke dressed in a delicate blend of green tea and dashi. This is TenTo’s high-impact take on Japanese brunch fare, informed by its mastery of soup stocks, specialty coffee and hand-whisked matcha. Try the snack menu with crisp katsu eggplant and house made miso cheese; opt for the minimalist Mont Blanc, finished with clouds of Hokkaido-style vanilla cream; and return for dinner (with sake) when you invariably want more. Good to know: Co-owner Ryota Kumasaka makes those gorgeous rough-hewn ceramics, and you can purchase them to take home. 3/8 Hill St, Surry Hills , tento.com.au Yum Yum Bakery



It’s not often a cafe can celebrate its 35th birthday, but family owned Yum Yum Bakery is one of the exceptional few. The milestone prompted big moves – a second location in Concord, a new contemporary look in Guildford – and though there’s more seating than ever, they’re all taken come lunchtime. It could be its food, a joyous expression of wood-fired Lebanese brunch fare. It could be its evolution, embracing modernity while maintaining tradition. But more than anything, it’s the warmth of its people – no matter who you are, you are welcome. Good to know: The hospitality is as outstanding as the food at this 2026 Good Food Guide cafe of the year winner. 273 Guildford Road, Guildford, yumyumbakery.com.au Related Collection Explore Good Food’s Essential Sydney Cafes and Bakeries 2026



Good Food reviews are visited anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries guide. Can’t see your favourite cafe? Chances are it’s in another category. Explore the full list of the 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries of 2026 in the Good Food app.

World.title: Hani Watson is in ‘24/7, bone-cracking pain’. She won bronze anyway
World.content:
SportCommonwealth Games Hani Watson is in ‘24/7, bone-cracking pain’. She won bronze anyway Hannah Kennelly July 25, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Para powerlifter Hani Watson is familiar with pain. So much so, she’s given it a nickname. “I call it Nigel and Nigel is always there,” she laughed. The para athlete was born with bilateral metaphyseal dysplasia, which bowed her tibia and femur bones and means she has to live with “24/7 bone cracking pain”. In the past year, Watson has had multiple surgeries on her legs to help deal with it. Hani Watson wins bronze for Australia. Getty Images But on Friday evening in Glasgow, Watson, a bronze medallist at Birmingham in 2022, banished “Nigel” to secure bronze again with a 147-kilogram lift in front of a roaring crowd at the SEC Armadillo.



“It’s still very surreal,” she said afterwards, proudly wearing her medal and a beaming smile. “It’s been a hard training session, hard sort of getting to where we are today. I didn’t actually think I was going to hit the numbers that coach asked ... but I just blocked it out. “I didn’t want to know, and I just went balls out and just hit it.” An emotional Watson after the event. Getty Images Watson started the competition well, easily clearing her starting weight of 140kg and briefly occupying the top spot on the leaderboard before Nigerian champion Folashade Oluwafemiayo lifted an extraordinary 165kg, setting a Commonwealth Games record.



Watson stayed steady, sitting on the bench with her eyes closed before letting out a warrior-like cry on her second attempt to clear 144kg and followed it with third lift of 147kg to secure third place. Dusting the chalk off her hands, she embraced her coach while the Aussies in the crowd leapt to their feet. Oluwafemiayo powered through a 175kg lift to set a world record and clinch gold, while Nigerian compatriot Rita Ferdinard rounded out the podium with a 158kg lift for silver Hani Watson with her bronze medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games. AP Strength runs in Watson’s blood. Her father Charlie was a bodybuilder who used to bicep-curl his daughter when she was younger. He would often tell Watson to “focus on your superpower” and bought her a gym membership when she was 10 years old. He died when she was just 17 years old.



Her mother died in 2023, and did not get a chance to see Watson compete in the 2024 Paralympics. Related Article Commonwealth Games Why netball survived intact as the Commonwealth Games shrank Watson said she thought of her parents right before she lifted the bar. “I sat the edge of that bench, and I said what my mum said to me, ‘You got this darling’. You know, I said to my mum and I said to my dad, ‘Help me lift this bar’ and they did exactly that.” Watson continued to reflect on her parents’ legacy and influence on her life.



“I believe in having that spirit, that energy, that mana, my culture that’s within me, the Australian spirit and just sitting there and calming myself down and listening to that internal voice,” she said. “As kids we don’t listen to our parents, but I’m listening to them now. And they told me, ‘This is your superpower, this is what you can do, this is what you need to focus on’.” The Queenslander’s Birmingham win broke Australia’s 16-year medal drought in the sport. She became the first Australian woman to medal in the event, and two years later qualified for the Paralympics in Paris. Watson has undergone at least a dozen operations over the past decade including double osteotomies on both legs – a surgical procure involving the cutting or reshaping of bones.



But in July 2025, Watson posted on social media telling her followers her pain had increased over the last six months, forcing her to “sedate and elevate” and rest, spending time with her dogs. “Not the life I saw happening, and it makes me hella nervous… but I get to still do something quite unique,” she posted. “And on the bright side, I don’t need legs to bench press!”



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Gold rush in the pool for Australia men and women take out 4x100m freestyle relays After several surgeries and some time off, Watson was back and in April she was named Australia women’s heavyweight representative for the Commonwealth Games. She won’t stop at winning bronze. Watson has the LA Paralympics in her sights and wants the Australian public and the world to keep backing para powerlifting. “I want to keep people excited about para powerlifting,” she said. ” It’s a very, very hard sport to do … So that’s a big dream of mine. “Getting to LA is another one, and then obviously back in Brisbane 2032, and ensuring that we’re setting up for a very good Para and Olympic Games.”

World.title: It took 48 years but this show has finally made it to Melbourne. It was worth the wait
World.content:
MUSICALS

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical ★★★★★

Victorian Opera, Union Theatre, until July 25

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical sets itself a challenge from the outset. First of all, which version of the much disputed Kelly story do you tell? Do you portray the famous outlaw as a folk hero or a villain? Then, once that is sorted, what tone should the whole thing have? After all, there are very real deaths and tragedies scattered throughout this story – and we all know how badly things turn out for the Kelly gang.

Luke London, Liam Head, Ethan Jones, Darcy Wain as the Kelly Gang. Casey Horsfield

This new production by Victorian Opera navigates all of this deftly. The story firmly has its flag planted in the folk hero camp, but does not gloss over the harsher realities of the story. The crimes are grounded in their context and the scenes slip from high-energy numbers to heart-wrenching grief with deceptive ease. It’s fun without ever being glib and serious without seeming insincere.

There are many times you’ll watch a musical, have a great time, then not be able to hum a single bar the moment you get home. That’s not the case here. In Ned Kelly the music is exceptional: memorable, eclectic and highly accomplished. Conductor Simon Holt – who also provided additional music and orchestration, necessary because there was no complete score of the original – conducts the Victorian Opera Chamber Orchestra with verve.

World.title: Gold, bronze and $30,000 in 50 minutes: The unexpected star of Australia’s big night in the pool
World.content:
SportSwimmingCommonwealth Games Gold, bronze and $30,000 in 50 minutes: The unexpected star of Australia’s big night in the pool Billie Eder July 25, 2026 — 7:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scroll down to see the medal tally after day one of the Commonwealth Games. Glasgow: Jenna Forrester wasn’t meant to swim in the women’s 200-metre backstroke at these Commonwealth Games. She originally missed out on a spot in the event after placing fourth at the Australian trials last month, and was given the late call-up when reigning champion Kaylee McKeown had to withdraw with glandular fever. Jenna Forrester shocked the field to win gold in the women’s 200m backstroke. Getty Images And yet, on Saturday morning (AEST) she found herself with a gold medal around her neck after stunning the field with a 2:08.17 swim – her second medal of the night after claiming bronze in the 400m freestyle just 50 minutes earlier.



“I did not expect that to happen tonight. I’m so over the moon,” Forrester said. “I didn’t really have much expectation going into the 400m free or the 200m backstroke, so I’m really happy with how that went ... I really just went into tonight with a positive attitude, and I felt like I had nothing to lose.” McKeown has dominated the event at every major meet since the Tokyo Olympics. The only time Forrester had raced internationally in the 200m backstroke was at the world championships in 2023, when she finished 10th. After tossing up whether she should start at all, given she thought she had a better chance in the 400m earlier in the night, she was ecstatic she had decided to go for it.



“I wasn’t sure if I was going to do the 200m backstroke because I thought I had a better shot at the 400m freestyle. But I spoke to my coach, and we just thought it’s a great opportunity,” Forrester said. “And I felt like I couldn’t turn down a swim at the Commonwealth Games because that’s pretty awesome. So yeah, I decided to do it, and I’m over the moon.” Jenna Forrester after realising she had won gold. AP Photo/Kin Cheung It was a sensational finish from Forrester, who was all the way back in fifth at the halfway point of the race – a position that had only improved to fourth by time she made the turn for the final 50m. “I spoke to my coach [Dean Boxall], and he said I had a very even split, and a lot of people said ‘you were really far behind at the 100m turn’,” Forrester said.



“I wasn’t really sure where I was in the field, but at the 100m mark I did have a sneaky look, and I was like ‘wow, I am really far behind’. But, I know the back end, especially in the 200m backstroke, is my strength as I am a 400m medley swimmer. “So that endurance work really comes in handy. It’s more seeing if I can catch up. I don’t always, but tonight I managed to.” Forrester is also now $30,000 richer because of Hancock Prospecting’s medal bonuses for Australian swimmers – $20,000 for winning gold and $10,000 for bronze. Her mother Louisa, who fought cancer two years ago, wasn’t poolside on Friday night. She was racing an ultra-marathon in Kyrgyzstan, but Forrester said that was who she got her fighting spirit from.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Aussie star says she was scared to reveal her Jewish identity at the Olympics. Now she’s found her voice again “She’s definitely the toughest person I know, and she’s probably my No.1 inspiration,” Forrester said. “To have a mother like that, even though she’s really tough herself, she is only ever supportive towards me, and I always know that no matter what my result is, she’ll always be proud of me.” Forrester still has the 200m and 400m individual medley to come, and said she’s setting her sights high after her results on day one. “I think I just need to approach the rest of my swims with the same mentality,” she said.

World.title: Mutiny on the golf course: Why members are threatening legal action against billionaire’s son
World.content:
NationalNSWInvestigation Mutiny on the golf course: Why members are threatening legal action against billionaire’s son Lucy Macken Updated July 25, 2026 — 7:03am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If Felix Ming Ze Lee, the 25-year-old son of beleaguered billionaire businessman Phillip Dong Fang Lee, is wondering what else could go wrong this week, members of the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club have bad news. As former Victorian premier Dan Andrews checked out the championship course earlier this week, more than 100 members of the privately owned, Lee-family controlled championship golf club have threatened legal action against the management amid claims of oppressive conduct and excessive annual subscription fee rises that they say are in breach of the club’s constitution. Former Victorian premier Dan Andrews checked out the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club this week. Artwork: Monqiue Westermann Fuelling heightened animosity among some members are falling resale values of membership shareholdings, and new joining, administration and registration fees, prompting members to describe it as now the only decent golf club in Sydney with a “waiting list of sellers”. The mutiny of members from the prestigious course caps off a tumultuous week for the young businessman. It started with dinner with the prime minister, only to be overshadowed days later by revelations about damning allegations from the tax office about his father’s “sham” financial arrangements to funnel huge sums of money from China to Australia.



An exhaustive investigation into the financial affairs of Phillip Lee has not only shed new light on the previously opaque origins of his wealth, but also included suspicions that the family patriarch continued operating his businesses in China decades after he told Australian authorities he had sold his business assets in China. “The [tax] commissioner believes that Mr Lee still has business and financial interest in the PRC [People’s Republic of China], notwithstanding his previous representations to the Australian government as part of his application for migration that all of his businesses in the PRC were sold,” states the tax office affidavit. Further, “those businesses appear to be held in structures which mask Mr Lee’s true ownership and control of those assets. In particular, the commissioner believes that Mr Lee has structured his financial affairs in such a way as to give the appearance that his mother and business associates are the owners of businesses which are in truth operated and owned by him”. More than 100 members of the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club have sent a legal letter of demand to the Lee family management. Wolter Peeters Felix Lee has sought to distance himself from his father’s business and financial affairs in recent years, founding the Lee Family Office, and inviting former federal treasurer and ex-ambassador to the United States Joe Hockey on as chairman.



Felix Lee declined to comment in response to questions about the tax office’s damning allegations about his father. “Phillip Lee’s tax affairs are his own and are not related to Felix Lee,” a spokesperson said on his behalf earlier this week. In response to inquiries about the legal letter, a spokesman for the club’s management said both parties are communicating in relation to their clients’ respective asserted, but contested, positions. Felix Lee’s week started with dinner with the prime minister and ended with a mutiny from members of his Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club. “The board has received legal correspondence, has considered the allegations carefully, and through its legal representatives has responded comprehensively, rejecting the allegations made,” the spokesperson said. “The company maintains that it has acted lawfully, in accordance with the club’s Constitution and its directors’ duties.” Central to Felix Lee’s responsibilities in recent years has been the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club, a prestigious championship course purchased by his parents from a syndicate of Japanese investors a decade ago.



Felix Lee was appointed director in November 2020, a few weeks after his 20th birthday, and more recently elevated to chairman. Fellow board members include his uncle Victor Lin, known among members as a passionate golfer, and Felix’s younger brother Edward Feng Zhao Lee, who was appointed early last year soon after his 19th birthday. Felix’s mother, Xiaobei Shi, stepped down early last year. Related Article Investigation The 25-year-old tasked with fixing billionaire father’s mess enlists help of Joe Hockey Former club member George Kalil didn’t know who Felix was when he first met him at a committee meeting at the club in about 2023, but he hasn’t forgotten it. “Felix Lee came in, unintroduced and totally unknown to me and other committee members,” Kalil said. “I thought he was there to take the coffee order, but he wasn’t the new waiter. He was Phillip Lee’s son, and he just launched into a tirade saying ‘you guys have to know your place’.” As Kalil and others understood it, things were set for a shake-up at the club. Among the changes, a member-elected committee was abolished three years ago and replaced with an advisory panel appointed by the Lee family directors.



While the original committee structure ostensibly allowed members some oversight of the club’s financial governance, the new advisory panel did not, according to members. Related Article Exclusive

Political donations Revealed: What really happened at the PM’s secretive Point Piper dinner A spokesman for the board said it believes the current structure improves effective member engagement because it has invited a more diverse cross-section of the membership base, including women, those with different playing skills and members who previously did not feel their views were being heard. When the Terrey Hills Golf and Country Club opened in late 1993 it was the first championship course built in Sydney in two decades. Wolter Peeters The members’ letter claims annual subscription fees have risen well beyond what they claim is the club’s constitution’s mandated cap of 5 per cent a year to total more than 20 per cent in the past two years.



The board rejected the claims of a constitution cap of 5 per cent on annual fees and said it wasn’t responsible for changes in membership resale values. “Subscriptions are determined depending upon working capital and expenditure of the club from time to time.” Claims from the membership that the board has imposed new member joining fee, administration fee and registration fee when a member tries to sell and transfer their shares were also rejected by the board, instead stating that the joining and administration fees have been in place since about 2000. In correspondence seen by this masthead, a founding member was revealed to have waited a year with no buyers before he recently sold his membership for $12,000, less than the club’s new joining fee of $12,500. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations ‘Sham’ loans, ‘unexplained’ wealth: Albanese dinner donor’s $260m family tax fight revealed One of the members who is currently on a waiting list to sell their stake in the club is James de Stigter, who paid about $45,000 to join. After injury left him unable to play for the past 18 months, he put his membership up for sale and expects it to sell for about $9000.



After Stephen Schinagel’s wife Heather Mead died, he made inquiries about putting her membership up for sale and was told late last year they were selling for about $20,000. It was a dramatic loss on the $65,000 she paid in 2017. It has since been discounted to $15,000 in a bid to hasten the process. “The market value of memberships is influenced by a range of factors, including broader economic conditions, discretionary spending, and market demand, and risks associated with membership were well documented in the several company prospectuses,” the spokesperson said. Members were hoping to flag their concerns at the annual general meeting held June 30, in particular about why annual fees increased given a $7.2 million cash reserve held by the club, but the opportunity never arose. Having opened the meeting, Felix Lee promptly announced there would be no dividend declared, and closed the meeting. Two minutes later, it was all over.
